date_end_year

Select items with an “event end date” in the given year:

date_end_year=2012

created_after

Filter resources to only show those that are created on or after the given date.

created_before

Filter resources to only show those created on or before the given date.

modified_after

Filter resources to only show those that are modified on or after the given date.

modified_before

Filter resources to only show those modified on or before the given date.

content_group

Select items which are member of the given content group (or one of its children):

content_group=public

name

Find resources with a matching unique name. A wildcard can be defined, for example:

name=page_*

Searching on an empty name or just * will return all resources with a defined name. The given name will be trimmed and converted to lowercase before searching.

language

Find resources with a certain language. The language must be a language code recognized by Zotonic, including supported regional variants. Search terms with invalid language codes are ignored.

Find all resources with a German translation:

language=de

Filter behaviour

Separate ordinary terms normally combine with AND. Some terms explicitly support OR lists, including filter and hasanyobject. The cat= filter: if you specify multiple categories, those categories are “OR“‘ed together, to allow to search in multiple distinct categories with a single search query.

Query resources

See also

  • mod_search reference: Zotonic’s built-in search module.

Query resources are, as the name implies, Resources of the special category query. In the admin this category is called “search query”. it is basically a stored (and thus content manageable) search query. You create an editable search query in an admin page that then is invoked from a template.

When creating such a resource in the page, you will see on the admin edit page an extra text field in which you can add search terms. Each search term goes on its own line, and the possible search terms are equal to the ones described on this page (the Query-model arguments).

properties.title: Connect to the running Erlang shell
properties.summary: From the checkout root:
properties.body:
From the checkout root:

bin/zotonic shell

This attaches to the live node. Expressions run against that node's actual code and data, so start with read-only inspection.

C = z:c(garden).
z_context:site(C).

Expect the site name garden. A fresh site context is not automatically an administrator context. Use an authenticated request context or deliberate, local-only elevation when testing mutations.

Leave the remote shell with Ctrl-C twice. Do not call q(). or halt(). to detach: they can stop the shared node.

If connection fails, check the target node name, Erlang distribution setup, and cookie configuration. See Work with a site context and Inspect content from the Erlang shell.

Inspect content from the Erlang shell

With C = z:c(garden) in an attached shell:

Id = m_rsc:rid(<<"page_home">>, C).
m_rsc:p(Id, title, C).
m_edge:objects(Id, haspart, C).

The named resource must exist on that site; undefined can mean the chosen name is absent. Use the generated site's real resource names rather than assuming every skeleton creates identical content.

Inspect individual properties first instead of dumping an entire resource containing private fields. Use models for normal content access, and understand the ACL context before interpreting missing results.

For a portable representation, inspect model#rsc_export. For changes, use model#rsc and model#edge, then check the public result separately. See Use stable resource names.

properties.title: Write logs that explain an operation
properties.summary: Log the operation and its result with structured fields. Include an identifier that helps connect the message to a resource or job, without logging credentials or complete private request data.
properties.body:
Log the operation and its result with structured fields. Include an identifier that helps connect the message to a resource or job, without logging credentials or complete private request data.

?LOG_ERROR(#{
    text => <<"Garden update failed">>,
    in => mod_garden,
    result => error,
    reason => Reason
}).

Use the logging macros from zotonic_core/include/zotonic.hrl when that header is already included. Branch on the actual result of the operation before logging success or failure.

Read logs and collect useful evidence

Access needed: Site log permission or server log access.

Container and host service logs may be stored in different places.

  1. Record the time, environment, hostname, affected page, and action that failed.
  2. Check the relevant site log or service log around that time.
  3. Identify the first relevant error and its module, request or correlation identifier, and repeated causes.
  4. Compare with the last deployment or configuration change.
  5. Reproduce once with safe test data when possible and note the expected and actual result.
  6. Share a short redacted excerpt and the reproduction steps with the responsible operator or developer.

Do not publish complete configuration dumps, cookies, authorization headers, password-reset URLs, or message bodies. Retain detailed logs in the controlled incident record.

More logging is not always better: temporary debug logging can expose data or fill disks. If enabled for diagnosis, record the change and turn it off afterwards.

properties.title: Installation and deployment
properties.summary: Prepare an environment and deploy a release with a recovery plan.
properties.body:
Prepare an environment and deploy a release with a recovery plan.

Choose a task below. Check its access requirement before starting, and verify the result with the intended account or service.

properties.title: Contribute a Zotonic change
properties.summary: Build the checkout, verify the change, and send a focused pull request.
properties.body:
Start with the repository's README, contributor instructions and current CI workflow. Use Erlang/OTP 28 for this documentation's development setup. Create a branch for one concrete change and keep unrelated formatting out of it.

  1. Reproduce the issue or describe the missing behaviour.
  2. Make the smallest maintainable change, following the surrounding Erlang and template conventions.
  3. Run the build and checks required by the checkout. Use a disposable test site for tests that change resources or schemas.
  4. Add a focused regression test when it verifies a meaningful behaviour.
  5. Update affected documentation and describe the observable result and validation in the pull request.

Current reference documentation is maintained with the relevant source; do not assume the former Sphinx import layout still owns every page. For module documentation, keep examples and zotonic_keywords aligned with the implemented API. Avoid promises about release dates or lint tools that are not part of the current repository workflow.

Report security-sensitive issues through the repository's security reporting policy rather than including an exploit or credentials in a public issue.

properties.title: Configure hostnames and HTTPS
properties.summary: Align DNS, site selection, and certificate termination.
properties.body:
Access needed: DNS and server configuration access.

  1. Decide the canonical hostname and required aliases. Make DNS point to the intended server or reverse proxy.
  2. Set the matching site hostname and aliases, and check the externally visible HTTP/HTTPS ports.
  3. Choose where TLS terminates: Zotonic or a reverse proxy. Install certificates through that component's supported mechanism.
  4. If using a proxy, forward the expected host and protocol information and support WebSocket connections. Keep direct backend access consistent with the deployment's access policy.
  5. Test the canonical URL and each alias, redirects, certificate hostname and chain, admin login, and a live browser interaction.
  6. Check certificate renewal and monitor expiry before it becomes an outage.

A working DNS record does not select the correct Zotonic site unless the hostname matches its configuration. A certificate working in your own browser is not proof that public clients trust it.

For a local first run, use the developer setup instructions. Production certificates, public redirects, and proxy settings need the actual deployment's reviewed configuration.

properties.title: Serve HTTPS on a privileged port
properties.summary: Terminate public traffic at a reverse proxy while Zotonic stays unprivileged.
properties.body:
Run Zotonic as an unprivileged service account on its configured high ports. Let the host's reverse proxy accept public HTTP/HTTPS and forward to a loopback or otherwise private backend. Verify that the backend is not accidentally reachable from the internet.

Configure the public hostname and advertised ports separately from listener ports. Trust forwarded headers only from the actual proxy addresses. Test redirect destinations, secure cookies, large uploads and MQTT/WebSocket connections.

If your deployment deliberately gives Zotonic direct access to a low port, use the operating system's narrowly scoped service capability mechanism and test it with the installed runtime. Avoid running the whole application as root or adding capabilities to a hard-coded beam.smp path that changes on every Erlang upgrade.

Do not copy interface-name parsing or firewall-redirection commands from old distribution recipes. IPv4, IPv6, containers and existing firewall policy all affect the result.

properties.title: Put Zotonic behind nginx
properties.summary: Forward HTTP and WebSocket traffic with a narrow trust boundary.
properties.body:
Configure Zotonic's backend listener on a private interface, for example loopback port 8000. Set the site's public hostname and HTTPS port to the values visitors use, and set proxy_allowlist to the actual proxy address(es). Consult zotonic.config.in for listener versus advertised-port settings.

In nginx's http context, define:

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    '' close;
}

Inside the site's existing TLS server block, with its real certificate and key:

location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
    client_max_body_size 100m;
}

This example assumes nginx is the single public proxy; it replaces an untrusted inbound forwarded-address header. A CDN or extra proxy hop needs an explicit trusted-chain configuration. Set the upload limit to your site's policy, and use the current nginx TLS defaults and your deployment's certificate policy instead of an old copied cipher list.

Run nginx -t before reloading. Test public pages, redirects, login, uploads and a WebSocket connection lasting beyond the usual HTTP idle timeout. Check the client address and scheme seen by Zotonic. nginx's WebSocket documentation explains the upgrade headers and idle timeout.

properties.title: Introduction to editing with Zotonic
properties.summary: Use the admin to keep your website up to date.
properties.body:
Zotonic lets you write pages, add images and files, and connect content. Your website decides how that content looks to visitors.

Start editing

  1. Open the admin address supplied by your website manager. It usually ends in /admin.
  2. Log in with your own account.
  3. Open All pages to find content, or Make a new page or media to create it.

You may see fewer options than the screenshots. Your account permissions, the page category, and the features enabled on your website determine what is available.

Saving a change to an already published page can make it visible immediately. Start with an unpublished practice page if you are learning.

If you cannot sign in

Use the password-recovery option on the sign-in screen if your site provides it. Follow the email instructions for your own account. If the message does not arrive, check spam and ask your website manager to confirm your account and email address. Some sites use an external sign-in service; use that service's recovery procedure.

After signing in, confirm that you can open All pages. Being signed in to the public website does not necessarily grant admin access. Sign out when you finish on a shared computer.

properties.title: Display images with mediaclasses
properties.summary: Define reusable image sizes in priv/templates/mediaclass.config and use them in image tags. For example, a local mediaclass can constrain an image's width:
properties.body:
Define reusable image sizes in priv/templates/mediaclass.config and use them in image tags. For example, a local mediaclass can constrain an image's width:

[
    {garden_card, [{width, 640}]}
].

{% image id mediaclass="garden_card" alt=id.title %}

Choose a meaningful description for an image when its purpose is not captured by the title. Check both portrait and landscape source images. Cropping is a design decision; do not add it automatically to every size.

Use model#media for media information and tag#image for rendering. See Work with uploaded media and Build and serve frontend assets.

Work with uploaded media

A media resource has ordinary content properties and information about its associated file. Use model#media to inspect and manipulate media through Zotonic's normal processing path.

Keep the archive file and generated previews separate in your reasoning. A missing preview can be a processing problem even when the original upload is present. Check the file's media type, processing status, and storage configuration before replacing the resource.

Use media APIs for replacement and deletion so derived files and notifications remain consistent. Do not construct archive filenames from titles. See Display images with mediaclasses, Configure persistent file storage, and An uploaded image does not display.

properties.title: Reuse markup with includes and categories
properties.summary: Extract repeated markup into a partial and pass its inputs explicitly.
properties.body:
Extract repeated markup into a partial and pass its inputs explicitly.

{% include "_garden_card.tpl" id=id %}

Inside the partial, read the resource using m.rsc[id]. Keep the partial focused on one component so another page can reuse it without inheriting unrelated page behavior.

Use a category include when the representation depends on the resource's category:

{% catinclude "_garden_card.tpl" id %}

Provide a generic fallback and add category-specific variants when their markup differs. Use the template selection tools to check which variant wins for the resource. See tag#include, tag#catinclude, and Find the template used by a page.

For the example above, save the fallback as priv/templates/_garden_card.tpl. An event-specific version is _garden_card.event.tpl. A resource named garden_open_day can override both with _garden_card.name.garden_open_day.tpl. Test an event and an ordinary text resource: the latter should still use the fallback.

Display values safely

Resource properties read through m.rsc follow Zotonic's content handling. Query arguments and values returned by custom models do not automatically have the same guarantees.

Escape plain text from those sources:

<p>{{ q.term|escape }}</p>

Do not mark arbitrary user input as safe HTML. Decide at the model or content boundary whether a field contains text, sanitized HTML, a URL, or another type. Keep that decision consistent across templates and API responses.

When a value renders unexpectedly, inspect its type and translation behavior before applying more filters. See filter#escape, Expose data through a model, and Keep permission checks at the boundary.

Override a module template

Find the active template and its path relative to priv/templates. Create the same relative path in your site or another active module with a higher selection priority.

Copy only the structure you need to change. When the original template offers blocks, extend it using the supported inheritance pattern rather than duplicating a large file. Check tag#overrules for extending the next matching template.

Load the affected page and inspect the selected template again. A successful compile does not prove that your override is used. Test neighboring categories and languages if the original template serves more than one page type.

For example, place this in the same relative template path as the template being overridden:

{% overrules %}
{% block content %}
    {% inherit %}
    <p>{_ Contact us for more information. _}</p>
{% endblock %}

Use a block that exists in the original. {% inherit %} keeps its content; omit it only when replacing that entire block is intentional. This is especially important for admin panels, where copying a small fragment over a large panel can remove controls.

properties.title: Use maintainable Zotonic patterns
properties.summary: Start with a working site, reusable templates and the standard media pipeline.
properties.body:
Build a small working site first, then add one capability at a time. Keep site-specific configuration in the site and reusable behaviour in a module. Use stable resource names in fixtures and import routines.

Keep template components small, pass values explicitly, and use resource/category selection instead of duplicating dispatch rules. Escape non-resource values in the correct output context. Render media through the image/media pipeline and named mediaclasses.

The connected tasks cover site creation, datamodel fixtures, template composition and media rendering. Test changes with the intended user's permissions and keep source separate from runtime files.

properties.title: Run Zotonic as a service
properties.summary: Start a foreground Zotonic process under the host service manager.
properties.body:
Use one service manager for each installation. On a Linux host with systemd, this is a starting point for /etc/systemd/system/zotonic.service:

[Unit]
Description=Zotonic
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=zotonic
Group=zotonic
WorkingDirectory=/srv/zotonic
ExecStart=/srv/zotonic/bin/zotonic start_nodaemon
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
TimeoutStopSec=120

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Adapt the account and paths to the installation. Ensure Erlang/OTP 28 and media tools are on the service's PATH, and that configuration and persistent storage are readable or writable by this account as appropriate. The process must run in the foreground; do not put bin/zotonic start behind Type=simple.

After reviewing the unit, run systemctl daemon-reload, enable/start it through your operating procedure, and inspect systemctl status zotonic and journalctl -u zotonic. Check a public page, login and an uploaded file. Test a restart and a host reboot in acceptance before production.

Keep secrets in the deployment's protected configuration. Containers should use their platform's restart and storage policies instead of a second systemd process inside the container. The old distribution-specific init scripts are historical examples, not the default installation route.

properties.title: Cache selected public assets with Varnish
properties.summary: Start with a narrow VCL 4 policy and preserve authenticated responses.
properties.body:
Use a supported Varnish installation and its matching VCL reference. Terminate HTTPS in the public proxy; Varnish's ordinary HTTP backend configuration does not itself provide that TLS endpoint. Keep the backend and management interface private.

Start with an explicit public asset policy. This VCL 4.1 example passes everything except anonymous requests under /lib/:

vcl 4.1;

backend default {
    .host = "127.0.0.1";
    .port = "8000";
}

sub vcl_recv {
    if (req.method != "GET" && req.method != "HEAD") {
        return (pass);
    }
    if (req.http.Authorization || req.http.Cookie || req.http.Upgrade) {
        return (pass);
    }
    if (req.url !~ "^/lib/") {
        return (pass);
    }
}

Let the built-in VCL process the remaining request and backend response. Do not strip Set-Cookie, override private/no-store responses, or force a positive TTL onto them. Keep media, API, admin, login and MQTT/WebSocket traffic out of this initial cache policy; the outer proxy should route WebSocket upgrades directly to Zotonic.

Validate the configuration with the installed Varnish version before loading it. Test an anonymous asset twice, then authenticated pages and a response with Cache-Control: private or no-store. Confirm only intended public content becomes a cache hit. Add page or media caching only after reviewing Zotonic's visibility, cache headers and invalidation requirements.

The old VCL 3 callbacks (vcl_fetch, vcl_error) and req.request field are obsolete. Use the current Varnish documentation for the version you deploy.

properties.title: Report a problem or request a feature
properties.summary: Give maintainers enough information to reproduce and assess the request.
properties.body:
Check whether the issue already exists in the Zotonic issue tracker. For a problem, describe the task, the steps you took, what you expected, and what happened. Include the Zotonic version or commit and relevant browser or server versions.

Use a small example and a screenshot when it makes the problem clearer. Remove passwords, tokens and private content from logs and images. For a feature request, explain the task it would help you complete and any current workaround.

An accepted issue is not a release-date commitment. Track progress in the issue or pull request. Follow the repository's private reporting instructions for security-sensitive problems.

properties.title: Creating a user
properties.summary: Set up an account when your role allows user management.
properties.body:
This task is for people allowed to manage accounts.

  1. Open the site's user overview, usually available from the admin navigation.
  2. Search for the person first. If they already have a person page, check its Username / password panel before creating a duplicate.
  3. Use Add user for a new person. Enter their name, email address, and the login details requested by the form.
  4. Complete the creation flow and check the resulting person page.
  5. Arrange the appropriate user-group membership with the website manager.
  6. Ask the new user to sign in and confirm that they can do their work.

Creating login details alone does not necessarily grant editorial permissions. Follow the site's account invitation and password procedures; do not put credentials in public page text or editorial notes.

This is a site-administration task. Before granting access, agree which content the person will maintain and whether they may publish, delete, or manage users. Verify with the new account that both the intended work and the expected restrictions apply. A successful administrator test does not check the new user's permissions.

Assign user groups and check access

Access needed: Site administrator with user-management and access-rule permissions.

Start with an existing account and a clear description of its work: which content it maintains, whether it publishes, and whether it manages other people.

  1. Find the person's page in the user overview and open it.
  2. In User groups, select the existing group that matches the agreed role. Check inherited memberships and save.
  3. Use a separate browser profile to sign in as a representative test account with those memberships.
  4. Check one allowed operation, such as editing a draft in the intended content group.
  5. Check one restriction, such as editing another team's content or opening user management.
  6. Record the membership change and the person responsible for approving it.

Do not give an account administrator access merely to fix one missing permission. If no existing role fits, have an access-rule administrator adjust the rules and test them before publication. More than one group can affect the effective permissions.

A person page, login identity, user group, and content group have different purposes. A collection used for navigation is not an access-control boundary.

Remove access when someone leaves

Access needed: Site administrator; identity-provider or integration access may also be needed.

First identify the person, the accounts they use, and which content or responsibilities need transferring.

  1. Review their user groups, collaboration memberships, API credentials, and any external sign-in method.
  2. Remove the memberships that grant access and save.
  3. For a local username/password account, open Set username / password and choose Delete Username. Read the confirmation carefully.
  4. Disable the account at an external identity provider and revoke separate integration tokens where applicable.
  5. Arrange invalidation of existing sessions with the site's authentication administrator; removing a password alone is not proof that every existing session is gone.
  6. Test that the former access methods fail and that the replacement owner can still do the work.

Keep the person resource when it is needed for authorship or records. Unpublishing a person page is not an account-deactivation procedure. Do not delete their content merely to remove a login.

The built-in admin account is configured separately; this username-deletion dialog does not manage it. Handle emergency administrator credential rotation through site configuration.

properties.title: Zotonic for editors
properties.summary: Practical help for writing, organizing, and publishing website content.
properties.body:
Use this guide to write, organize, and publish content in Zotonic's admin. Start with Getting started, or choose a collection below. Use Surveys and forms to collect feedback, take registrations, and follow up on responses.

The screenshots show the standard admin on a test website. Your site may use different labels, categories, or layouts. Some tools are available only when your website enables them and your account has permission.

Saving edits to a published page can update the website immediately. Use an unpublished page while learning or preparing new content.

properties.title: The Zotonic workspace
properties.summary: The checkout is an Erlang umbrella project: one build contains many applications.
properties.body:
The checkout is an Erlang umbrella project: one build contains many applications.

  • apps/ contains Zotonic's core applications and bundled modules.
  • apps_user/ contains your sites and additional modules.
  • apps_user/<project>/apps/ can contain applications in a nested project; this path is included in the current build configuration.
  • _build/ contains build output and dependencies. Do not treat it as the authoritative source directory.
  • doc/ contains versioned documentation and reference sources.
  • bin/zotonic is the command-line entry point.

A site or external module can be its own Git repository inside apps_user. Before changing files, check which repository owns them. Add dependencies in the appropriate rebar.config, then build from the umbrella root.

What belongs in src and priv

Use src for compiled Erlang code and priv for application resources.

Put request handling in controllers, model APIs in models, template transformations in filters, rendered components in scomps, and supporting business logic in support. Directory names help readers; the Erlang module name and exported callbacks still determine behavior.

Under priv, put routes in dispatch, templates in templates, browser-ready files in lib, and their editable build sources in lib-src. Translation catalogs belong in translations.

Do not put uploaded files, caches, or local secrets in a deployable assets directory. Use the site's configured storage and configuration mechanisms. Do not edit generated CSS when its source and build command are available.

Runtime data and uploaded files

Keep runtime data separate from the application's source and static assets.

Site media, generated previews, backups, logs, and caches can live outside the checkout. Their locations depend on the running installation's configuration. Use Zotonic's storage and path APIs rather than assuming a relative directory beside a template.

For media, work through model#media and related storage facilities so metadata, preview generation, access checks, and storage backends remain coordinated. Never replace a file behind the model's back as a normal upload workflow.

When deploying, preserve the site's durable files as well as its database. Rebuilding _build is not a backup or migration strategy for uploaded content.

properties.title: Add an HTTP controller
properties.summary: Use controller_template when a dispatch rule only needs to render a template. Write a custom controller when the endpoint needs additional request processing or response behavior.
properties.body:
Use controller_template for a page that only renders a template. For a public, read-only plain-text endpoint, create src/controllers/controller_garden_hello.erl in the active Garden application:

-module(controller_garden_hello).
-export([content_types_provided/1, process/4]).

-spec content_types_provided(Context) -> {Types, Context}
    when Context :: z:context(), Types :: list().
content_types_provided(Context) ->
    {[{<<"text">>, <<"plain">>, []}], Context}.

-spec process(Method, Accepted, Provided, Context) -> {Body, Context}
    when Method :: binary(), Accepted :: term(), Provided :: term(),
         Context :: z:context(), Body :: binary().
process(_Method, _Accepted, _Provided, Context) ->
    {<<"Welcome to the garden">>, Context}.

Add a rule to the application's priv/dispatch/garden list:

{garden_hello, ["garden-hello"], controller_garden_hello, []}

Compile, refresh discovery, and request /garden-hello on the site's hostname. Expect a plain-text response containing the greeting. Check dispatch if it returns another page. The rule above is one tuple inside the dispatch list, not an entire dispatch file.

This example deliberately returns public constant text. Private data needs explicit authorization callbacks and model checks; a write endpoint also needs method handling, input validation, and protection against unauthorized requests. Consult controller#controller_template for a built-in alternative and controller#controller_api for model-based HTTP access.

properties.title: Get Zotonic
properties.summary: Choose a release or a development checkout and follow the installation guide.
properties.body:
Use Zotonic releases for a tagged release. Read its requirements and upgrade notes before using it with an existing database.

For a development checkout:

git clone https://github.com/zotonic/zotonic.git
cd zotonic

Then follow the local-environment guide: choose containers, a native installation, or Nix; prepare dependencies; build; start; and create a practice site. This documentation advises Erlang/OTP 28. Use a supported PostgreSQL major release that meets Zotonic's requirements, with its current maintenance updates.

Do not treat the old 1.0.0-rc.7 download link as the current release, or use the unauthenticated git:// clone URL from older instructions.

properties.title: Render template values safely
properties.summary: Choose escaping for the value and the output context.
properties.body:
Template output is not universally auto-escaped. Treat request values, custom model results and external data as untrusted.

For ordinary text and quoted HTML attributes, escape at the output:

<p>{{ q.search|escape }}</p>
<input name="search" value="{{ q.search|escape }}">

Request values can also have unexpected structured shapes. For resource lookups, resolve a scalar identifier and use m.rsc[value].id; do not trust arbitrary request data as a resource object. Check authorization on the server before reading private data or changing a resource.

Persisted resource properties normally pass through Zotonic's resource sanitization. This allows intentional rich text such as id.body to render as HTML. That does not make every custom model, raw database value or import option safe. Do not apply an HTML-stripping bypass to untrusted content.

JavaScript, CSS and URLs require their own handling. Prefer generated element IDs and the {% javascript %} pipeline instead of interpolating text into scripts. Use a JSON encoder when sending JSON. HTML escaping alone cannot prevent an unsafe URL scheme; accept only the schemes and destinations your feature supports.

Test a literal <script> string, quotes, ampersands, unexpected list/map input and a javascript: URL at each relevant boundary. Expect text to stay text and invalid input to be rejected. A CSP is an additional boundary, not a replacement for correct encoding and validation.

Display values safely

Resource properties read through m.rsc follow Zotonic's content handling. Query arguments and values returned by custom models do not automatically have the same guarantees.

Escape plain text from those sources:

<p>{{ q.term|escape }}</p>

Do not mark arbitrary user input as safe HTML. Decide at the model or content boundary whether a field contains text, sanitized HTML, a URL, or another type. Keep that decision consistent across templates and API responses.

When a value renders unexpectedly, inspect its type and translation behavior before applying more filters. See filter#escape, Expose data through a model, and Keep permission checks at the boundary.

To make those look like your own design it is useful to know which classnames are used. This is a short overview of most of the classes used in these standard components.

properties.title: Getting started
properties.summary: Find your way around the admin and make your first change.
properties.body: Find your way around the admin and make your first change.

properties.title: The admin interface
properties.summary: Know where to find pages, editing controls, and settings.
properties.body:
The admin is the part of your website used to manage content.

  • Dashboard shows recent changes and shortcuts to pages and media.
  • Content opens content overviews and tools available on your site.
  • Search helps you find existing pages.
  • The edit page contains the title, summary, body text, attached media, and connections.
  • Save, Save and View, and Published control saving and publication.

On the current admin, the right-hand side has Connected to, Connected from, and Settings & more tabs. Open Settings & more for the publication period, page settings, and optional tools. Older versions may show these panels directly.

Click a panel heading to expand it. Use View to open the website version of a saved page. Some content types have no public page of their own.

properties.title: Your first page
properties.summary: Create, check, and publish a simple page.
properties.body:
Use this short exercise for a new page that you are allowed to publish.

  1. On the dashboard, click Make a new page or media.
  2. Enter a clear title and choose the appropriate category, such as Text.
  3. Leave Published unchecked and click Create page.
  4. Write a short summary and a few paragraphs in Content.
  5. Click Save, then View to check the saved page while logged in.
  6. Return to the edit page, check Published, and click Save when the page is ready.
  7. Open the page in a private browser window to check what a visitor sees.

Publication also depends on the publication period and access settings. A new page does not automatically appear in a menu.

Check before sharing

Read the saved page on a narrow screen. Follow every link and check that images have useful descriptions. If a private window shows a login page or an error, finish the publication and access checks before sharing the address. For a practice page, unpublish it when the exercise is finished.

properties.title: Finding content
properties.summary: Find a page without creating a duplicate.
properties.body:
1. Open All pages from the dashboard.
  2. Search for a distinctive word from the title.
  3. Use the category and other available filters to narrow the results.
  4. Open the matching page for editing. Check the title and category before changing it.

If you cannot find the page, clear the filters and try a shorter search. A page may have a different title in another language or belong to an unexpected category. The dashboard also lists recently modified content.

Your permissions limit which results you can see. Ask your website manager for the page link if you still cannot find it. Search for an existing image in All media before uploading another copy.

properties.title: Understanding pages and content
properties.summary: Recognize the different kinds of content you can edit.
properties.body:
A page can be an article, a person, an event, an image, or a collection. Zotonic calls each of these a resource.

When you create content, choose its category. The category describes what it is and can change the fields you see and its appearance on the website.

Content can be connected. For example, an article can have an author, keywords, and attached images. These are separate pieces of content that can be reused.

To understand an existing page, check its category under the title and its Connected to and Connected from tabs. You do not need to understand the technical data model to edit its text.

properties.title: Creating and editing content
properties.summary: Write clear pages, add links and blocks, and manage changes.
properties.body: Write clear pages, add links and blocks, and manage changes.

properties.title: Creating a page
properties.summary: Start a new page with the right category and language.
properties.body:
1. Click Make a new page or media on the dashboard or the creation button in a content overview.
  2. Enter the title. Check the suggested existing pages to avoid a duplicate.
  3. Choose the category that matches the content.
  4. If offered, choose the content group and language. Ask your website manager if you are unsure about the group.
  5. Leave Published unchecked while drafting.
  6. Click Create page, add your text, and Save.

The available categories depend on your permissions. Choose a category for what the content is, rather than where you want it to appear. Menus and collections handle placement.

properties.title: Editing a page
properties.summary: Change existing content and check the result.
properties.body:
1. Find the page in All pages and open it for editing.
  2. Check the title, category, and language tab.
  3. Change the fields you need.
  4. Click Save and wait for the saved confirmation.
  5. Click View, or use Save and View, to check the result on the website.

Changes in the form are not saved until you save them. Connections and menu changes can save separately, so do not assume that leaving the form cancels every action.

If the page is already published, saving can update the public version immediately. Agree on timing with other editors before making a major change. Zotonic does not provide a separate pending draft of every published page by default.

If saving reports an error, keep the form open and copy your new text somewhere safe before reloading. Resolve the reported problem and wait for a successful save. If another editor has changed the page meanwhile, compare their saved version before replacing it.

properties.title: Titles, summaries, and body text
properties.summary: Put each part of your text in the right field.
properties.body:
• Title names the page. Make it specific enough to recognize in search results and menus.
  • Summary gives the main point in one or two sentences. Your site may use it in lists, previews, or introductions.
  • Content contains the main body text.
  • Short title, when used by your site, provides a shorter label for navigation or lists.

Write the title first, then a summary that helps the reader decide whether to open the page. Use short paragraphs and descriptive subheadings in the body.

Save and view the page. A field can be stored correctly without appearing in your site's design. If a summary is missing from the public page, check with your website manager before copying it into several fields.

properties.title: Formatting text
properties.summary: Make body text easy to scan and read.
properties.body:
1. Place the cursor in Content, or select text to change.
  2. Use Formats for a paragraph or heading. Choose headings by their place in the text, not just their size.
  3. Use the list buttons for steps or a set of related items.
  4. Use bold or italic sparingly.
  5. Save and check the public page, including on a narrow screen.

When pasting from another document, use your editor's plain-text paste option or Clear formatting if unwanted styles appear. Reapply headings and lists with the toolbar.

Use the page title as the main heading and start body sections below it. Avoid empty paragraphs or repeated spaces to position content: the layout changes between devices.

properties.title: Adding links
properties.summary: Link readers to another page, website, or email address.
properties.body:
Link to a page on this site

  1. Select meaningful link text in the body.
  2. Click Insert an internal link.
  3. Find and select the destination page in the chooser.
  4. Save the page and test the link.

Use the internal chooser when possible so the link identifies the Zotonic page.

Link to another website or email address

Select the text and click Insert/edit link. Enter the full website address, including https://, or an email link such as mailto:info@example.org. Confirm the dialog and save.

Use link text such as “View the opening hours” rather than “click here”. Check that the destination is accessible to your readers; your editor account may be able to open private pages that visitors cannot.

properties.title: Adding content blocks
properties.summary: Add structured sections when your site provides them.
properties.body:
Some sites use blocks for sections such as text, a quote, media, or a linked page. The available block types and their appearance are set by the website.

  1. Open the page for editing.
  2. Click add page block below the main content.
  3. Choose a block type and fill in its fields.
  4. Use the block controls or drag handle to arrange the blocks, if available.
  5. Save and view the page.

A block containing a page or image usually refers to existing content. Removing that block is different from deleting the referenced page or media item.

If the block you need is missing, ask your website manager which type to use. A block appearing in the admin does not guarantee that every page layout displays it.

properties.title: Changing the category of a page
properties.summary: Change the kind of content without making a new page.
properties.body:
1. Open the page and save any text changes.
  2. Click the category link below the page title.
  3. Choose the new category in the dialog and confirm the change.
  4. Check the available fields, connections, and public appearance.

Choose the category here. Leave the content group unchanged unless you also intend to change how the page is managed.

On the current admin, Settings & more also offers Change category and/or content group. A content group controls how content is managed; it is not the same as its category.

Changing category can change the page layout and where it appears in lists. Only select a category that fits the content. If you only want to add a topic such as “Gardening”, use a keyword instead.

properties.title: Duplicating or reusing content
properties.summary: Choose between a new copy and a connection to existing content.
properties.body:
Reuse an existing image, document, or page when it should stay the same wherever it appears. Add it through a media chooser, menu, collection, or connection.

To make an independent page:

  1. Open the original and save any changes.
  2. Choose More → Make a duplicate, or Duplicate… under Settings & more.
  3. Review the dialog, enter the new title, and create the copy.
  4. Check its text, languages, publication settings, and connections before publishing.

A duplicate is a separate page. Editing its text does not update the original. Connected media may still be shared; do not assume that duplication makes independent copies of every image and file.

properties.title: Deleting content
properties.summary: Remove a page that is no longer needed.
properties.body:
If a page should only disappear from public view, unpublish it first. Deletion removes the content itself and can affect menus, links, and connected pages.

  1. Open the page and check its Connected from tab or Referrers link.
  2. Arrange replacements for links or menu entries that still need a destination.
  3. Choose Delete… under More or Settings & more.
  4. Read the dialog carefully and confirm only when it names the intended page.
  5. Check the affected parts of the website.

A protected page cannot be deleted until its protection is removed by someone allowed to do so. Recovery depends on the site's backup features and retained data. Do not rely on a universal trash folder or assume that media files can be recovered.

properties.title: Viewing and restoring earlier versions
properties.summary: Recover an earlier saved version when revision history is available.
properties.body:
1. Open the page and select Settings & more.
  2. Expand Backup & Restore.
  3. Click List and restore an earlier version.
  4. Compare the saved versions and select the one you need.
  5. Review the restore confirmation, restore it, and check the current page.

Select two saved versions to compare them. Added text is highlighted in green and removed text in red. Comparing versions does not restore one.

This feature must be enabled on your site. If the panel is missing, ask your website manager for help.

Restoring an earlier version replaces current page content. Coordinate with other editors so their recent work is not lost. Revision history is not a complete backup of every connection and media file. Check attached media, menu entries, and connections separately after recovery.

properties.title: Adding an editorial note
properties.summary: Leave a short note for other editors.
properties.body:
Use a note for information such as “Check the opening hours before publishing”. It is separate from the page's public body text.

  1. Open the edit page.
  2. Click Add note near the save controls, or Edit note if a note exists.
  3. Write a short, specific message and save it in the note dialog.
  4. Update or remove an outdated note when the work is finished.

A note is an aid for editors, not an approval workflow or a task assignment system. Do not put passwords or sensitive information in it. Other people who can edit the page may be able to read it.

properties.title: Publishing
properties.summary: Control when a page is available and who can see it.
properties.body: Control when a page is available and who can see it.

properties.title: Publishing and unpublishing
properties.summary: Make a page available or take it out of public view.
properties.body:
Publish

  1. Open the page and check the saved content.
  2. Check Published beside the save controls.
  3. Check the Publication period under Settings & more.
  4. Click Save.
  5. Test the public page in a private browser window.

The publication period must include the current time, and the visitor must have access.

Unpublish

Clear Published and click Save. The page stays in the admin for later editing. Editors with sufficient permissions may still see it.

Saving and publishing are different actions. However, saving edits to an already published page can update it immediately. Unpublishing does not recall downloaded files, emails, or copies already stored elsewhere.

properties.title: Publication dates
properties.summary: Understand the dates that control availability.
properties.body:
Open Settings & more → Publication period on the edit page.

  • Visible from is the start of the publication period.
  • Visible till is the end of the publication period.
  • Publication date of original article records an original publication date; it does not replace the visibility period.

Check the date and time together. Use the page's Time zone panel if the timing is unclear. A future start or an expired end can keep a page from visitors even when Published is checked.

The separate Date range panel describes the content itself, such as an event's start and end. Changing an event date is not the same as scheduling publication.

After editing publication dates, click Save and check the result with a visitor account or private window.

properties.title: Scheduling a page
properties.summary: Prepare a page to appear at a future time.
properties.body:
1. Finish and save the page.
  2. Open Settings & more → Publication period.
  3. Set Visible from to the intended start date and time.
  4. Set Visible till only if the page should stop being available at a particular time.
  5. Check the time zone and ensure the end follows the start.
  6. Check Published and click Save.

Before the start, the page should be unavailable to ordinary visitors. After the start, check its public URL and the lists or menus where it should appear.

You are scheduling the page's availability, not a separate version of its text. This does not schedule individual edits to an existing published page. Scheduling an email mailing is a separate task.

To cancel a scheduled publication, clear Published and save. To publish now, also change a future Visible from date to the intended current or past time. Check Visible till as well: an expired end still prevents publication. Recheck the public URL after either change.

properties.title: Who can see a page?
properties.summary: Check publication and access separately.
properties.body:
A visitor can see a page only when its publication state, publication period, and access rules allow it.

  1. Check Published and the publication period.
  2. Open Settings & more and inspect the page's content group and any access controls your site shows.
  3. Ask your website manager if the page belongs to a restricted group or you do not have permission to change its access.
  4. Test as the intended audience: use a private window for public content, or a suitable test account for member content.

Show private properties to controls fields such as private contact details. It is not a general switch for making the whole page public.

Removing a menu entry or asking search engines not to index a page does not restrict access to its URL.

properties.title: Previewing content
properties.summary: Check a saved page before visitors see it.
properties.body:
Some content types have no standalone public view. Check them on the page where the website uses them.

  1. Save your changes.
  2. Click View or Save and View.
  3. Check the title, text, images, links, and layout.
  4. Return to the editor to correct anything that needs attention.

Your editor account may show unpublished or restricted content. Being able to preview it does not mean that visitors can see it. To check public availability, use a private browser window after publication.

Preview shows saved content. Keep Published unchecked while drafting a new page. Saving changes to an already published page may update the live page before you preview it.

properties.title: Removing a page from the website
properties.summary: Choose the right way to remove content.
properties.body:
Decide what should disappear:

  • To stop ordinary visitors seeing a page, clear Published and save.
  • To remove a navigation link, remove the menu item.
  • To stop listing a page in a collection, remove that collection connection.
  • To remove the content itself, use Delete… after checking its referrers.

After the change, check the old public URL and any relevant menus or lists in a private browser window. If another page replaces it, ask your website manager about a redirect.

A page can still be accessible even when no menu links to it. Search engines and outside websites may also retain links or copies for a while.

properties.title: Keeping a page out of search engines
properties.summary: Request that search engines leave a page out of their results.
properties.body:
1. Open the page for editing.
  2. Expand SEO Content.
  3. Check Ask Google to not index this page.
  4. Click Save.

This is an indexing request to search engines that respect it. It can take time for an already indexed page to disappear. It does not hide the page from visitors, restrict its URL, or necessarily remove it from your site's own search.

Use publication and access settings for content that should not be public. If the checkbox is missing or the page still appears in search results later, ask your website manager to check the site's search-engine settings.

properties.title: Media
properties.summary: Upload, reuse, and display images, documents, and video.
properties.body: Upload, reuse, and display images, documents, and video.

properties.title: Working with media
properties.summary: Understand where images and files are stored.
properties.body:
An image or file is a separate content item. A page can use it as attached media, an attachment, or an image inside its body text. Several pages can use the same item.

Before uploading, search All media for an existing copy. Reusing it keeps its title, description, and file in one place.

Choose how to use it:

  • Attached media supplies images for the page layout, such as a lead image or gallery.
  • Insert media item in the text editor places media at a particular point in the text.
  • A document connection or link helps readers open or download a file.

Your website decides which connections it displays and how. Always view the page after adding media.

properties.title: Uploading an image
properties.summary: Add a new image to the media library.
properties.body:
1. Open All media and choose the upload or new-media action. You can also upload through add media item on a page.
  2. Open the Upload tab and select the image file.
  3. Enter a useful title, such as “Volunteers planting at the community garden”.
  4. Review the available publication and content-group options, then complete the upload.
  5. Open the resulting media item and check the image, description, and any credit or license information.

Use a sharp original that you have permission to publish. The website normally creates smaller display versions for you. Your account may have limits on file types and upload size.

Uploading to the media library does not by itself place the image on a particular page.

properties.title: Adding an existing image
properties.summary: Reuse an image instead of uploading a second copy.
properties.body:
1. Open the page that needs the image.
  2. Under Attached media, click add media item.
  3. Use the chooser's search to find the image by title.
  4. Check its preview and choose the existing media item.
  5. View the page to confirm that the correct image appears.

If you need the image inside a paragraph, use Insert media item in the text editor instead.

The same media item can serve several pages. Replacing its file may change all those uses. If another page needs a different crop, caption, or image, check which settings apply only to this use before changing the shared item.

properties.title: Adding an image to a page
properties.summary: Attach a lead image or other media used by the page layout.
properties.body:
1. Open the page for editing.
  2. Find Attached media and click add media item.
  3. Select an existing image or upload a new one.
  4. Check the list of attached items. If the list supports dragging, put them in the required order.
  5. Save any text changes and view the page.

An attached image is connected to the page. The site design decides whether to show it as a lead image, gallery, thumbnail, or something else. Some designs use the first suitable image.

If the image should appear at an exact place in the body text, insert it through the text editor. An attachment alone does not place it between paragraphs.

properties.title: Adding images in rich text
properties.summary: Place an image between or beside paragraphs.
properties.body:
1. Place the cursor at the intended position in Content.
  2. Click Insert media item in the editor toolbar.
  3. Find an existing image or upload a new one, then select it.
  4. Select the inserted image to open its media properties when you need to adjust it.
  5. Save the properties, save the page, and view the result.

The properties can include a caption, alignment, size, crop, and link. Their final appearance depends on your website.

Use Remove from text in the media properties to remove this use of the image. That does not delete the media item from the library or remove it from other pages.

properties.title: Image captions and alignment
properties.summary: Adjust an image inserted in the body text.
properties.body:
1. Open the media properties for an image in Content.
  2. Enter a Caption if the reader needs context or a credit.
  3. Choose Between text, Aligned left, or Aligned right.
  4. Choose a size and use Crop image only when the crop suits the subject.
  5. Save the dialog and page, then check the result at both wide and narrow screen sizes.

In the standard rich-text media dialog, an empty caption uses the media summary. Enter a single - to suppress the caption for that use.

A caption is visible text beside an image. It is different from alternative text used to describe the image when it cannot be seen. The available sizes and crop behavior depend on the site design.

properties.title: Replacing an image or file
properties.summary: Update a media item while keeping the item itself.
properties.body:
1. Find the image or document in All media and open it.
  2. Check Connected from or Referrers to see which pages use it.
  3. Use the media replacement or upload action offered on its edit page.
  4. Select the new file and complete the replacement.
  5. Check the media item and the pages that use it.

Replacing the file changes the shared media item. Other pages using that item can show the replacement too. Upload a separate item if only one page needs a different file.

Check its title, summary, credits, and accessibility information after replacement. For a document, also test the download link. A browser or external service may temporarily show a cached copy.

properties.title: Uploading documents
properties.summary: Offer a PDF or another file for readers to download.
properties.body:
1. Upload the file through All media or a page's media chooser.
  2. Give the document a title that describes its contents.
  3. Connect it to the page using the document or attachment connection your website displays, or add a link through the internal link chooser.
  4. Save the page and test the link as a visitor.

Use link text that tells readers what they will get, for example “Download the garden handbook (PDF)”. The site's link or document layout determines whether the file opens directly, downloads, or opens a document page.

Check that the file is readable and accessible before publishing. If the document contains private information, ask your website manager to check access to the file as well as to the page linking to it.

Open the uploaded file through the page link, rather than checking only the original on your computer. Confirm that it is the intended version and that its text can be selected and searched. A scanned image of a document may need a text version. Include the file type and, for large downloads, the size in the link description.

properties.title: Adding video and other embedded media
properties.summary: Add supported online media or a video file.
properties.body:
1. Open the new-media or media-connection dialog.
  2. Choose Website or Embed to use a supported video's public URL, or Upload for a video file if your site allows it.
  3. Complete the dialog and inspect the new media item.
  4. Attach it to a page or insert it in the body with Insert media item.
  5. Save and check playback on the public page.

Uploaded video may need processing before it is ready. An online embed depends on the provider allowing it and the video remaining available. Cookie-consent settings can also delay loading an embed.

Use captions or provide a transcript where needed. If a provider or file type is unsupported, ask your website manager which format to use.

properties.title: Finding media
properties.summary: Locate the right file in the media library.
properties.body:
1. Open All media from the dashboard.
  2. Search by a distinctive word in the media title.
  3. Use available category filters, such as image, video, or document.
  4. Open the item and check its preview, title, and file details.

If you know a page that uses the file, open that page and follow the attached media or document connection. Check the text editor too: an image inside the body may be used separately from the page's lead image.

Your permissions affect which media items appear. Avoid uploading a new copy until you have checked the existing library and cleared any search filters.

properties.title: Removing media
properties.summary: Remove an image from one page or delete the shared item.
properties.body:
To remove a single use, remove the item from Attached media, remove its document connection, or choose Remove from text for an image in the body. Then check the public page.

To delete the media item itself:

  1. Open it in All media.
  2. Inspect Connected from or Referrers and check known uses in body text.
  3. Replace or remove any uses that should continue working.
  4. Use Delete… and read the confirmation.

Deleting shared media can break several pages. Connection lists may not reveal links copied manually into text or used outside this website. If you only need a different image on one page, change that page's connection instead.

properties.title: Making images understandable
properties.summary: Provide useful text for readers who cannot see an image.
properties.body:
Describe the information an image contributes. For example, “Raised beds beside a wheelchair-accessible path” is more useful than “garden photo” when the page discusses access.

  1. Give the media item a meaningful title and summary.
  2. If your site's image form has an alternative-text field, fill it for the image's purpose on that page.
  3. Use a visible caption for context or credits that all readers need.
  4. Ask your website manager how the site creates alternative text if the field is not available.

The standard rich-text media dialog has a caption field, but does not offer a separate alternative-text field in every setup. Do not assume that adding a caption also sets the image's alternative text.

Put essential instructions in normal text too. Decorative images should not add distracting descriptions; how to mark them depends on the site.

For a chart, put the important figures or conclusion in the surrounding text. For an image used as a link, describe the destination or action. Avoid repeating a long caption as an image description. After saving, have the website manager check the rendered alternative text if you cannot verify it with your site's preview tools.

properties.title: Organizing content
properties.summary: Use categories, keywords, connections, and collections to organize pages.
properties.body: Use categories, keywords, connections, and collections to organize pages.

properties.title: How Zotonic organizes content
properties.summary: Choose the right tool for organizing a page.
properties.body:
Use each tool for a different purpose:

  • A category says what the content is: an article, person, image, or event.
  • A keyword says what it is about: gardening, education, or local history.
  • A connection links it to another item, such as an author or related article.
  • A collection groups selected items in an order.
  • A menu provides navigation for visitors.

Start by creating the page in the right category. Add existing keywords and connections where they help readers find related content. Put the page in a collection or menu when the website calls for it.

Changing one of these does not automatically change the others. A published page can exist without a menu entry or collection membership.

properties.title: Choosing categories
properties.summary: Describe what kind of content a page contains.
properties.body:
Choose a category when creating a page. On an existing page, its category appears below the title.

Use the most appropriate available category. For example, use an event category for an event rather than using an ordinary text page just because it contains text.

Categories can control the edit fields, public layout, search filters, and permitted connections. If a category is missing, your account may not be allowed to create it.

Use keywords for topics that can apply to many kinds of content. Avoid creating a new category just to group a few related pages. Ask your website manager before changing the category structure: it affects the whole site.

properties.title: Adding keywords or tags
properties.summary: Connect a page to its subjects.
properties.body:
1. Open the page and look in Connected to for Keyword, Subject, or your site's equivalent label.
  2. Click add and search for an existing keyword.
  3. Select the keyword that matches the topic.
  4. Repeat for other useful topics and check the resulting connections.

Use the site's established spelling. Search before creating a new keyword so “Garden” and “Gardening” do not accidentally become competing labels. Create a new keyword only when your role and editorial guidelines allow it.

A keyword connection does not guarantee that a tag appears on the public page. Your website may instead use it for related content or filtering. Removing the connection leaves the keyword available for other pages.

properties.title: Connecting pages
properties.summary: Link an article to an author, subject, or another page.
properties.body:
1. Open the source page for editing.
  2. In Connected to, find the type of connection you need and click add. Use Add connection for other available types.
  3. Search for the destination page and check its preview.
  4. Select it, then check that it appears under the intended connection type.
  5. View the public page to see how the site uses that connection.

Choose the connection type, then search for the destination. In this example, selecting “Community garden visit” would connect the article to the survey.

For example, connect an article to a person under Author. This records an authorship relationship; it is different from putting a text link in the article.

Connection changes can be saved immediately. Use Connected from on the destination to see incoming connections. The site design determines which relationships it displays.

To correct a connection, remove the incorrect relationship and select the right destination. This removes the connection, not the destination page. Reopen Connected to to confirm the saved result. Do not add a reverse connection merely to make it appear under Connected from: Zotonic already shows incoming connections there.

properties.title: Featured and related content
properties.summary: Suggest which pages deserve attention.
properties.body:
To mark a page as featured, check Featured near the save controls and click Save. Your website must be designed to use this flag before it changes what visitors see.

For related content, open Connected to and add the relationship your site uses, such as Relation or References. Select the related page and check the public result.

Some sites choose related content automatically from shared keywords. If the displayed suggestions do not match your manual connections, ask your website manager how that section works.

Featured status does not publish a page, add it to a menu, or grant access. Related pages still need suitable publication and access settings for the intended readers.

properties.title: Creating and using collections
properties.summary: Group pages into an ordered set.
properties.body:
A collection is useful for a guide, a series, or a group of related pages.

Adding a page to a collection reuses the page; it does not copy its text. A page can belong to more than one collection.

  1. Create a page in the Collection category and give it a clear title and introduction.
  2. Open its collection editor or its outgoing Has part connections, depending on your site's admin layout.
  3. Add the existing pages that belong in the collection.
  4. Arrange them in the intended reading order.
  5. Check the collection and each member's publication settings, then view the result.

Your site decides how to display the collection, its children, and any previous/next navigation. A collection does not automatically become a navigation menu.

To remove a member, remove its Has part connection from the collection; do not delete the member page. Reopen the collection to confirm the order was saved. Keep nested collections free of loops: a collection should not contain itself, directly or through another collection. Check a reused page in each collection where it appears.

properties.title: Changing the order of content
properties.summary: Put connected pages or media in the intended sequence.
properties.body:
1. Open the collection, menu, or page that contains the ordered items.
  2. Use its drag handles or ordering controls to move the items.
  3. Follow any save action shown by that editor.
  4. Reload the edit view to check that the order was stored, then check the public page.

Menu and connection editors can save order changes immediately. A text form's Save button is not always what stores those changes.

An order belongs to a particular list or connection. Moving a page within one collection does not necessarily move it in another. Some public lists sort by date or title instead of your manual order; ask your website manager if the result differs.

properties.title: Understanding relationships
properties.summary: Read outgoing and incoming page connections.
properties.body:
Open a page's Connected to tab to see the content it points to. Open Connected from to see the content that points to it.

For an article connected to a person as its author:

  • On the article, the person is an outgoing Author connection.
  • On the person, the article appears as an incoming connection.

The connection name tells you what the relationship means. Direction matters: “this article has this author” is different from “this person has this article as an author”.

Use Connections or Referrers near the page title for a wider overview. Before deleting shared content, inspect its incoming connections. A text link or external use may not be represented in these lists.

properties.title: Menus and navigation
properties.summary: Help visitors move through your website.
properties.body:
Help visitors move through your website.

These tasks apply when your website offers this feature and your account has access to it.

properties.title: Editing the main menu
properties.summary: Find the menu that your website displays.
properties.body:
1. Open Content → Menu if that shortcut is available, or find the menu page in All pages.
  2. Check that you are editing the main menu rather than a footer or another menu.
  3. Inspect the menu tree and add or move items as needed.
  4. Reload the editor to check the saved structure.
  5. Check the public navigation, including on a narrow screen.

Menu changes can be saved as you make them. Do not assume that closing the editor cancels a move.

Your site may use a different navigation setup. If there is no menu editor, ask your website manager which content controls navigation. Creating a menu resource alone does not make the website display it.

properties.title: Adding a page to a menu
properties.summary: Create a navigation entry for an existing page.
properties.body:
1. Open the intended menu.
  2. Click Add menu item, then choose Add top or Add bottom, or use an existing item's menu to add nearby.
  3. Search for and select the page.
  4. Move the new item to its intended position.
  5. Check the menu on the website as a visitor.

The menu refers to the page; it does not duplicate it. Check that the page is published, within its publication period, and accessible to the intended audience. A menu entry for an unavailable page may be hidden or lead to an inaccessible page, depending on the design.

A page can be published without belonging to a menu.

properties.title: Moving menu items
properties.summary: Change the order and position of navigation entries.
properties.body:
1. Open the menu editor.
  2. Drag an item up or down to change its order.
  3. Keep it at the same indentation if it should stay on the same level.
  4. Drop it and check the tree before moving another item.
  5. Reload and check the public menu.

Dragging left or right can change the parent and create a submenu. Moving a parent may move its nested items with it, so inspect the whole branch.

If the public order does not match, confirm that you edited the correct menu. A site's navigation may be built from a collection or another source instead.

properties.title: Creating submenus
properties.summary: Place a menu entry under another entry.
properties.body:
1. Add both the parent page and child page to the menu.
  2. Drag the child below the intended parent and slightly to the right.
  3. Check the indentation: it should show the child nested under that parent.
  4. Add more children if needed.
  5. Check the public menu on desktop and mobile.

To return a child to the top level, drag it left until it aligns with the other top-level items.

The public menu design decides how many nested levels it supports and how visitors open them. Keep the structure shallow enough to understand. The menu hierarchy does not itself change a page's category, URL, or access permissions.

properties.title: Removing a menu item
properties.summary: Remove a navigation entry while keeping its page.
properties.body:
1. Open the menu editor.
  2. Open the relevant menu item's controls and choose its removal action.
  3. Check what happens to any nested items before completing the removal.
  4. Reload the editor and check the public menu.

Removing the menu item does not delete or unpublish its page. People may still reach that page through its URL, search, another menu, or a link.

If the page itself should become unavailable, open it separately, clear Published, and save. If it has a replacement, consider updating links and arranging a redirect as well.

properties.title: Working with multiple menus
properties.summary: Keep main, footer, and section navigation separate.
properties.body:
A site can have several menu pages, each with its own tree.

  1. Find the menu page by its title or category in All pages.
  2. Confirm where the website uses it: main navigation, footer, or a section.
  3. Edit its items and check that specific area of the website.

The same content page can appear in more than one menu. Removing it from one menu does not remove it from the others.

Ask your website manager before creating a new menu for the public site. The design must be configured to display it. Give menu pages clear names so editors can tell them apart, and use their links when coordinating changes.

properties.title: Languages and translations
properties.summary: Maintain several languages on the same page.
properties.body:
Maintain several languages on the same page.

These tasks apply when your website offers this feature and your account has access to it.

properties.title: Working with multilingual content
properties.summary: Understand what is shared and what is translated.
properties.body:
A multilingual page keeps its translations together. You normally edit one page with language tabs, rather than create a separate page for each language.

Fields such as the title, summary, and body can have a value for each language. Other properties and connections may be shared. Check the language label beside a field before changing it.

  1. Open the page and choose its language tab.
  2. Edit the translated fields.
  3. Save and view the page in that language.
  4. Repeat for other languages that need updating.

Changing the admin interface language does not translate your content. A language tab also does not prove that every field has been translated or reviewed. Check the whole page, including captions and linked documents.

properties.title: Translating a page
properties.summary: Add and review text in another language.
properties.body:
1. Open the page and save any current changes.
  2. Click + Translate.
  3. Choose From existing language and To new language.
  4. Choose Copy texts, Leave texts empty, or Automatic translation if available.
  5. Click Add translation.
  6. Open the destination language tab, translate or review every field, and Save.
  7. View the page in that language and test its links.

Copying provides a starting point; it does not translate the text. Automatic translation needs editorial review too. When offered, it sends the text to the configured translation service.

Existing destination text is preserved unless you select Overwrite existing texts with new translations. Use that option carefully.

On an already published page, saving a translation can expose the new text immediately. Agree on a review process before copying untranslated text into a language offered to visitors. Check shared fields and connections separately: changing an image or publication setting may affect every language.

properties.title: Seeing which languages a page has
properties.summary: Check available languages and translation completeness.
properties.body:
Open the edit page and look at its language tabs. Click + Translate to see Current translations.

For each language:

  1. Open its tab.
  2. Check the title, summary, body, and any other translated fields.
  3. Use Show translations if available to compare the texts.
  4. View the public page in that language.

A listed language means it is associated with the page. It does not mean that every field is filled, that an automatic translation is accurate, or that the public website offers that language.

If a needed language is absent from the choices, ask your website manager whether it is enabled for editing and publication.

properties.title: Adding or removing a translation
properties.summary: Manage the languages of an individual page.
properties.body:
To add a language, click + Translate, choose the source and destination languages and a method, then click Add translation. Review the new text and save the page.

To remove one:

  1. Save any changes you want to keep.
  2. Open + Translate and find the language under Current translations.
  3. Click its Delete translation control and read the confirmation.
  4. Save the page to store the removal.

Removing a language hides it from the form first. Saving then deletes its translated text from the page. Do not use this as a temporary “hide this tab” action.

The other language versions remain on the same page. Check the public language switch and any language-specific links afterwards.

properties.title: Copying content between languages
properties.summary: Use existing text as a starting point for a translation.
properties.body:
