1. Save the page and click + Translate.
  2. Choose the source language and the destination language.
  3. Select Copy texts.
  4. Leave Overwrite existing texts with new translations unchecked to fill empty destination fields only.
  5. Click Add translation, edit the copied text into the target language, and save.

Select overwrite only when you intend to replace existing destination text. Check all affected fields before saving.

Copying text does not keep the two languages synchronized. Later changes to the source need a separate update in the translation. Shared images and connections may not need copying, but captions or language-specific documents still need checking.

properties.title: Missing translations and fallback languages
properties.summary: Understand why a page may show text in another language.
properties.body:
If a translated field is empty, the website may use text from another language. This is called a fallback. The site's settings and templates determine when that happens.

  1. Open the page's language tab in the admin.
  2. Check whether the relevant field contains a translation.
  3. Add the missing text and save.
  4. View the page using the public language switch.

If the wrong language still appears, check whether the text belongs to a connected image, person, document, or another page. Those items may need their own translations.

Ask your website manager about fallback rules and languages available to visitors. Do not create duplicate pages simply to work around a missing translation.

properties.title: Language-specific URLs
properties.summary: Check links to translated content.
properties.body:
Use the public language switch to open a page in the required language, then copy its URL if you need to share it.

A language code such as /en/ or /nl/ may appear in the address. The remaining path or title slug can also vary by language, depending on the site's configuration.

  1. Translate and save the page.
  2. View it in each public language.
  3. Check the address and test any links you plan to share.

Use the internal page-link chooser when linking within the site. Avoid manually adding language prefixes to arbitrary URLs. If a translated address needs changing, follow your site's URL policy and check existing links and redirects afterwards.

properties.title: People and access
properties.summary: Understand editorial accounts, permissions, and shared work.
properties.body: Understand editorial accounts, permissions, and shared work.

properties.title: Users and editors
properties.summary: Understand the difference between a person page and an account.
properties.body:
A person page can describe an author or contact without giving that person permission to log in. A user has login details or another sign-in identity.

An editor is a user whose permissions allow editing particular content. Being able to log in does not automatically give access to all pages or admin tools.

Use your own account so colleagues can see who changed a page. Ask your website manager to arrange the right access for each new editor.

If you manage users, check existing person pages before creating a new one. Avoid duplicate profiles for someone who already appears as an author. Keep public biography information separate from private contact and account details.

properties.title: What am I allowed to edit?
properties.summary: Understand why available actions differ between editors.
properties.body:
Your account's permissions can control whether you can create, view, edit, publish, delete, or upload particular content. They can depend on category, content group, ownership, and group membership.

Start with the content you have been assigned. If a button is missing or disabled, do not assume the website is broken.

When requesting access, send your website manager the page link and the action you need, such as “edit the summary” or “upload a PDF”. This is more useful than asking for full administrator access.

Access to edit a page and access to view it as a visitor are different. Check public availability separately when publishing.

properties.title: Why can’t I edit this page?
properties.summary: Check your account and the page before requesting help.
properties.body:
1. Check that you are logged in with the intended account.
  2. Open the page in the admin, not only its public view.
  3. Check whether editing is unavailable for the whole page or only for a field or action.
  4. Note the category and content group, if visible.
  5. Send the page link and the missing action or error message to your website manager.

The page may belong to another content group or be managed by an import. Your role may allow reading but not editing, or editing but not deleting.

Deletion protection is different from permission to edit text. Do not make a duplicate just to bypass a restriction: it can leave conflicting versions on the site.

properties.title: Content ownership
properties.summary: Know who created content and who is responsible for it.
properties.body:
The edit page shows when content was created and modified, and by whom. This helps you find the last editor when coordinating a change.

The creator, the last editor, the connected author, and the person responsible for maintaining a page can be different people. Changing an Author connection does not automatically transfer editing rights.

  1. Check the page history shown near the title.
  2. Check any editorial note and relevant connections.
  3. Agree with the responsible editor before replacing substantial content.
  4. Ask your website manager to change ownership or group access when needed.

Avoid editing the same page at the same time as another person. Save and communicate completed changes so someone else does not overwrite them with an older form.

properties.title: Collaboration groups
properties.summary: Work with a group when your site supports group-based content.
properties.body:
Some sites use collaboration groups to bring people and content together. Group membership can affect what members or managers can see and edit.

  1. Open the relevant group using the site's navigation or a link from your manager.
  2. Check that you are a member with the right role.
  3. Create or edit content within the group's intended area.
  4. Check the audience before publishing or sharing a link.

A collaboration group is different from a collection of public pages. Do not assume that connecting a page to a group makes it private. The site's access rules determine that.

Ask a group manager or website manager to resolve missing membership or permissions. The available group screens vary between sites.

properties.title: Upload restrictions
properties.summary: Resolve a rejected file upload.
properties.body:
If an upload fails, read the message before trying again.

  1. Check the file size and actual file type.
  2. Check that the file opens correctly on your computer.
  3. Use a format and size accepted by your website.
  4. If the error concerns permission, tell your website manager which type and size you need to upload and where it belongs.

Upload limits can depend on your account or group. A file extension alone does not make a file an allowed type. Renaming a file to look like an image or PDF will not fix its contents.

If processing fails after an upload, keep the original and report the media item's link and the error. Avoid creating many duplicate uploads while the first one is still processing.

properties.title: Mailing lists and newsletters
properties.summary: Prepare, test, send, and follow up on email mailings.
properties.body:
Prepare, test, send, and follow up on email mailings.

These tasks apply when your website offers this feature and your account has access to it.

properties.title: Working with mailing lists
properties.summary: Choose the audience for an email mailing.
properties.body:
A mailing list holds or selects recipients. A mailing uses a content page as the email to send to that audience.

  1. Open Mailing lists in the admin.
  2. Find the intended list and check its title and purpose.
  3. Open its recipients or list settings as needed.
  4. Prepare the content page separately before starting a mailing.

Some lists use individual addresses; others also use connected people or a saved query. Check how your list selects people before sending. The total subscribers shown initially can differ from the eligible count after language, subscription, and delivery-history checks.

These tools are available only when mailing features and the relevant permissions are enabled. Follow your organization's subscription practices when adding people.

properties.title: Managing recipients
properties.summary: Keep a mailing list accurate.
properties.body:
1. Open the list's Recipients view.
  2. Search or filter by address, status, or language as needed.
  3. Use the recipient controls to add or edit an address and its details.
  4. Check whether the recipient is enabled and which language they prefer.
  5. Save the change and check the list again.

A subscribed address is not the same as a user account. Creating or editing a recipient does not give that person access to the admin.

Respect unsubscribe choices. Do not re-enable an address simply because it is missing from a mailing's eligible audience. It may be disabled, blocked, invalid, or excluded by the language or delivery-history options.

properties.title: Creating a mailing
properties.summary: Prepare the page that will become your email.
properties.body:
1. Create or open the content page you want to send.
  2. Write a clear title and concise body. Add suitable images and meaningful links.
  3. Save the page.
  4. Open Settings & more → Mailing list and choose Preview mailing.
  5. Check the email layout and send a test before selecting the full audience.

An email can look different from the website page because it uses an email layout. Check links, image availability, and the unsubscribe information in the actual email.

Keep the intended recipients and language versions in mind while writing. Editing a page after sending does not change messages already in people's inboxes.

properties.title: Sending a test mailing
properties.summary: Check an email with a small, controlled test.
properties.body:
1. Save the content page and open its Mailing list panel under Settings & more.
  2. Choose Send test email, or use the test controls within the mailing dialog.
  3. Enter your test address and choose the language if offered.
  4. Send the test and inspect it in an email client.
  5. Check the title, text, images, links, layout, and footer. Correct the page and test again if needed.

A test can be sent immediately even when the page is unpublished, provided you can view it. A successful test does not prove that the full audience settings are right.

Before a full send, review the actual list, language selection, eligible count, previous-delivery option, and timing separately.

properties.title: Sending a mailing
properties.summary: Review the audience and email before the full send.
properties.body:
1. Save the page and complete a test mailing.
  2. Choose Send mailing from the page's Mailing list panel.
  3. Select the intended mailing list.
  4. Choose the email language and audience options. When using recipients' preferred languages, check the fallback and exclusion choices.
  5. Review Previous deliveries. Sending again to everyone can produce duplicate emails.
  6. Preview the email and continue to the review step.
  7. Check the eligible recipients, language, and timing, then confirm the send using the final action shown.
  8. Open the mailing run to follow its progress.

The initial subscriber total is only an estimate of the audience. The review step applies eligibility checks. After sending, messages already delivered cannot be recalled by unpublishing the page.

properties.title: Scheduling a mailing
properties.summary: Choose when an email mailing should start.
properties.body:
1. Save and test the mailing page.
  2. Start Send mailing and choose the list, language, and audience.
  3. In the timing section, choose the option offered for publication or Send the mailing on a specific date and time.
  4. Enter the intended time and check the displayed time zone.
  5. Review the audience and schedule before confirming.
  6. Check the mailing's status afterwards to confirm that it is scheduled.

Publication-based sending depends on the page becoming published and reaching its publication start. A specific-date mailing has its own schedule; inspect the review step for any publication requirements.

To change a scheduled mailing, use the scheduling or cancellation controls shown on its status screen. Do not assume that editing an event date or unchecking Published cancels an already created mailing run.

After cancelling or rescheduling, reopen the run and check its recorded state and time. If it has already started, cancellation may stop only work still pending; messages already handed to a mail server can still arrive. Ask your website manager for help if the status does not confirm the change.

properties.title: Checking mailing status
properties.summary: See what happened after a mailing was started.
properties.body:
1. Open View mailing history from the page's Mailing list panel, or open All mailings from the dashboard.
  2. Select the relevant run, checking the page, list, language, and start time.
  3. Read its status, progress, and recipient outcomes.
  4. Inspect failures before retrying or sending again.

A queued message has not necessarily been sent. A message accepted by a mail server has not necessarily reached the inbox or been read. Use the labels and details on the run to distinguish those outcomes.

If retrying, review the previous-delivery options so people do not receive unintended duplicates. Give your website manager the run link and error details when delivery appears stuck or fails repeatedly.

properties.title: Importing and exporting recipients
properties.summary: Transfer a list of email addresses.
properties.body:
1. Open the mailing list's Recipients view.
  2. Use its upload/import action and read the format instructions.
  3. Prepare the file exactly as requested. The standard recipient view describes one email address per line; do not assume it accepts an arbitrary spreadsheet.
  4. Review any replace, remove, or update options before importing.
  5. Inspect the resulting recipients and their status.

Use the download/export action when you need a local copy. Store it where only the intended people can access it.

Import only recipients who belong on that list. An import is not a reason to undo previous unsubscribe choices. If you need names or language preferences as well as addresses, check the import dialog's supported format with your website manager.

Try a small file containing only addresses approved for the test before importing a large list. Compare the recipients before and after the import, including disabled addresses and duplicates. If the dialog offers replacement, use it only when the uploaded file is intended to become the complete list. An exported file is not proof that all recipient preferences can be restored by importing it again.

properties.title: SEO and sharing
properties.summary: Help people recognize and find your pages.
properties.body:
Help people recognize and find your pages.

These tasks apply when your website offers this feature and your account has access to it.

properties.title: SEO basics for editors
properties.summary: Make useful pages easy to understand and discover.
properties.body:
Start with the content: a specific title, a clear introduction, useful headings, and descriptive links help readers find their way.

Before publishing:

  1. Check that the page answers a real reader question.
  2. Give it an accurate title and concise summary.
  3. Link to it from relevant pages, menus, or collections.
  4. Check its public URL, image, and language versions.
  5. Review the page-level SEO Content fields if your role uses them.

SEO fields provide information to search engines; they do not guarantee a ranking or a particular search-result snippet. Avoid repeating keywords unnaturally. Ask your website manager about site-wide search settings rather than changing unfamiliar technical fields.

properties.title: Page titles and descriptions
properties.summary: Write a useful title and description for search and sharing.
properties.body:
Search engines can shorten or replace the supplied title and description, so do not rely on a fixed character count to guarantee their display.

  1. Open the page and expand SEO Content.
  2. Use Page title when the browser or search title needs to differ from the content title.
  3. Write a concise Page description that accurately summarizes the page.
  4. Check each language you maintain.
  5. Save and view the public page.

Keep the main message near the start.

When these fields are empty, your site may use the ordinary title and summary. The fallback depends on the design. Leave technical fields such as custom structured data to the people responsible for the site's implementation.

properties.title: Search engine visibility
properties.summary: Distinguish public access from search indexing.
properties.body:
A public page is not necessarily indexed, and a previously indexed page can remain in search results after a change.

To request exclusion, open SEO Content, check Ask Google to not index this page, and save. To allow indexing again, clear the option and save, then ask your website manager to check any site-wide or category-level restrictions.

The Hide page from searches option under Advanced, if available, concerns site queries that respect it. It is separate from search-engine indexing.

Neither option is access control. Use publication and permissions for private content. Search engines choose when to revisit a page, and a site's sitemap or indexing settings may also affect discovery.

properties.title: Social sharing information
properties.summary: Check how a page looks when its link is shared.
properties.body:
Social platforms may use the page's title, description, and image to build a link preview.

  1. Check the main title and summary, and any SEO Content overrides.
  2. Attach a suitable image in the place your website uses for sharing images.
  3. Save and make sure the page and image are publicly accessible when intended.
  4. Test the link using the platform's preview or inspection tool before sharing it widely.

The exact fields used depend on your website. Ask your website manager if the wrong image or text is selected.

Platforms cache previews. Editing the page may not update an existing preview immediately. Avoid repeatedly replacing the image until you have checked whether the platform is still using an old copy.

properties.title: Changing page URLs
properties.summary: Understand slugs and paths before changing an address.
properties.body:
A page's address can include a title-based slug or a custom page path.

  1. Open the saved page with View and note its current URL.
  2. If your role allows it, use Customize page slug under SEO Content for the title-like part of the address, or Page path under Advanced for a custom path.
  3. Use a short, clear value and follow the site's naming conventions.
  4. Save and test the new address in each relevant language.
  5. Test the old address and arrange a redirect if it no longer reaches the right content.

Changing a title does not mean every site's URL changes in the same way. Avoid changing Unique name or Unique uri as a way to edit the public address: those fields have other purposes.

properties.title: Redirecting an old address
properties.summary: Help readers reach replacement content.
properties.body:
A redirect sends visitors from an old address to a current destination. It is useful when pages move or content is replaced.

  1. Record the old URL and the exact replacement URL.
  2. Check whether the old address already redirects correctly.
  3. Ask your website manager to configure a redirect if your admin has no dedicated redirect tool.
  4. Test the old address in a private browser window and check that it reaches the intended page.
  5. Update links and menu entries you control to use the current destination.

Do not send every removed page to the home page: choose a relevant replacement when one exists. Avoid redirect loops and destinations that visitors cannot access. Redirect tools and automatic handling of old paths vary by site.

properties.title: Common tasks and troubleshooting
properties.summary: Find the cause of common editing and publishing problems.
properties.body: Find the cause of common editing and publishing problems.

properties.title: My changes don’t appear on the website
properties.summary: Check saving, language, and the page being displayed.
properties.body:
1. Return to the edit page and confirm that the change was saved successfully.
  2. Check that you edited the intended page and language.
  3. Use View from that page instead of an old bookmark.
  4. Reload the public page and compare it in a private window.
  5. Check whether the visible content comes from a connected page, block, image summary, or another field.

Some designs do not display every admin field. A summary, featured flag, or connection can be stored without appearing in the current layout.

If the result is still wrong, give your website manager the edit link, public URL, changed field, language, and approximate save time. Mention whether the problem also appears in a private window.

properties.title: Why can’t I find a page?
properties.summary: Clear filters and check access before creating another copy.
properties.body:
1. Open All pages and clear category, language, publication, and other filters.
  2. Search for a short, distinctive part of the title.
  3. Check other language titles if the site is multilingual.
  4. Look in All media if the item is an image or file.
  5. Follow a known edit link or ask another editor for the page URL.

An unpublished page may be absent from public search but available in the admin. Your account may also lack permission to see it. A renamed or deleted page will not necessarily appear under its old title.

Do not immediately create a replacement: that can produce duplicate content. If the page was deleted, ask about recovery first.

properties.title: Why isn’t my page published?
properties.summary: Check the controls that determine visitor access.
properties.body:
1. Check Published and click Save.
  2. Open Settings & more → Publication period.
  3. Check that Visible from is not in the future and Visible till has not passed.
  4. Check the time zone if the timing is unexpected.
  5. Ask your website manager to check the content group and access rules.
  6. Test the public URL in a private window.

If the URL works but the page is missing from a menu or list, publication may be correct. Check menu membership, collection connections, category, and any filters used by that list.

Being able to view a page while logged in as an editor is not proof that visitors can see it.

properties.title: Why isn’t an image showing?
properties.summary: Check the media item and how the page uses it.
properties.body:
1. Open the media item and confirm that the upload or processing completed.
  2. Check that the intended page has the image under Attached media, or that it was inserted into the body text.
  3. Save the page if you changed its body.
  4. Check the media item's publication and access settings.
  5. View the page in a private window.

Your website may display only certain connections or the first image in a list. Uploading a file to the library alone does not put it on a page.

For online media, check that the provider still allows the embed and whether cookie consent is required. Report the page and media links to your website manager if the item works in the admin but not publicly.

properties.title: Why is the wrong image showing?
properties.summary: Find which image source the page layout uses.
properties.body:
1. Open the page and inspect Attached media.
  2. Check the order and remove unintended connections rather than deleting shared images.
  3. Check images inserted in the body and any media blocks.
  4. Open the selected media item to see whether its file was replaced.
  5. Save relevant edits and check the public page.

The site may use the first attached image, an image from connected content, or a separate sharing image. Ask your website manager which source the layout uses if it is unclear.

If the website is correct but a social preview is wrong, the platform may be showing a cached preview. Check that before changing the page again.

properties.title: Why does another language show old content?
properties.summary: Update the translation and check fallback text.
properties.body:
1. Open the page's language tab for the language that looks wrong.
  2. Compare the relevant fields with the source language.
  3. Translate the changed text and save.
  4. View the public page in that language.

Translations are separate text values. Editing English does not automatically rewrite Dutch, even if Dutch was originally copied from English.

If the field is empty, the site may use fallback text from another language. If the old text belongs to an image caption, menu item, or linked page, inspect that content too.

Use the public language switch when testing so you know which version you are viewing. Check the browser address and the page title.

properties.title: Why isn’t my page in the menu?
properties.summary: Check navigation separately from publication.
properties.body:
1. Confirm that the page is present in the menu your website actually uses.
  2. Check its position and indentation; it may be nested under another item.
  3. Check that the page is published, within its publication period, and accessible to visitors.
  4. Reload the menu editor to verify the saved structure.
  5. Test the public menu on both desktop and mobile.

Creating or publishing a page does not automatically add it to a menu. A page can also belong to a collection without appearing in navigation.

If the editor tree is correct, ask your website manager whether the navigation uses a different menu, hides certain categories, or limits submenu depth.

properties.title: I accidentally changed or deleted something
properties.summary: Take the next step without overwriting more content.
properties.body:
For unsaved text edits, use the editor's undo command or leave the form without saving if you are sure you do not need the changes. This does not undo connections or menu actions already saved separately.

For a saved page, check Settings & more → Backup & Restore → List and restore an earlier version if available. Compare the versions before restoring.

For deleted content or missing media, contact your website manager promptly. Give the old URL or title and the approximate time of the change. Recovery depends on enabled backups, retained revisions, and whether the file still exists.

Check related menus, connections, and media after recovery. Restoring page text is not necessarily a complete restoration of everything that used it.

properties.title: A link is broken
properties.summary: Find and repair the link at its source.
properties.body:
1. Open the page containing the broken link and copy the destination for comparison.
  2. Check whether the destination was renamed, moved, unpublished, restricted, or deleted.
  3. For an internal page, replace the link using Insert an internal link when possible.
  4. For an external website, check the current address with its owner or public site.
  5. Save and test the link as a visitor.

If the broken link is in a menu or collection, edit that structure instead of the body text. For a file, check the media item and its download link.

If outside websites still use an old URL, ask your website manager about a redirect. Fixing one link on your site does not update links elsewhere.

properties.title: Understanding Zotonic
properties.summary: Learn the few concepts that make everyday editing easier.
properties.body: Learn the few concepts that make everyday editing easier.

properties.title: Pages and resources
properties.summary: Understand why people, images, and articles share an editor.
properties.body:
Zotonic stores an article, person, event, image, or collection as a resource. The admin often calls these pages because they share editing tools.

For a technical explanation, see model#rsc in the developer reference.

A resource has properties such as a title and category. It can also have media and connections to other resources.

Not every resource has a useful public page of its own. An image may be displayed inside an article, and a keyword may mainly be used to organize search results.

When editing, focus on the content's purpose and the page where visitors use it. A stored field or connection is only shown publicly if the website's design uses it.

properties.title: What categories mean
properties.summary: Separate a content type from a topic or a folder.
properties.body:
A category describes what a resource is. Examples include person, event, image, and article.

A page belongs to one category, which can sit below a broader category. For example, an article can be a kind of text. This hierarchy helps the website select fields, layouts, and lists.

A category is not a folder that determines the page's location in a menu. It is also not a tag: use keywords to describe topics that cross content types.

When choosing a category, ask “What is this content?” For “Where should it appear?”, use a menu, collection, or the site's listing rules.

The technical reference is model#category.

properties.title: What connections mean
properties.summary: Understand how separate content works together.
properties.body:
Developers call connections edges and connection types predicates. See model#edge for the technical reference.

A connection records a named relationship from one resource to another.

For example, an article can point to a person as its Author, a keyword as its Subject, and an image as its Depiction. The admin may show friendlier labels, such as Keyword or Attached media.

Connections have a direction. The article is connected to its author; the person's page can show that the article is connected from it.

A connection is different from a link typed into a paragraph. It gives the website structured information that can be used in layouts, lists, and related content.

properties.title: Media and depictions
properties.summary: Understand shared files and page images.
properties.body:
For developers, see model#media.

A media resource is an item with an image, document, audio, video, or embed attached to it. It has its own title, properties, and access settings.

A depiction connection says that an image or media item represents another page. The admin commonly shows these items under Attached media. The site might use them as lead images or thumbnails.

Media can also be inserted into rich text. This lets an editor choose a position within the body. Attaching an image to the page and inserting it in the body are separate uses.

Because the media item is shared, replacing its file can affect several pages. Removing one connection normally leaves the media resource available elsewhere.

properties.title: Menus and collections
properties.summary: Choose navigation or an ordered group of content.
properties.body:
A menu is a navigation tree. Its entries can have children, allowing submenus. The website's design chooses which menu to display and where.

A collection groups resources through Has part connections. It can represent a guide, series, or other ordered set. A collection can contain another collection when the site supports that structure.

Both reuse existing pages. Neither duplicates their text or automatically publishes them. A page can appear in several collections and menus.

Use a menu when the goal is navigation. Use a collection when the goal is to present related content as a set. The website may display collection navigation too, but that is a design choice.

properties.title: How languages work
properties.summary: Understand translated fields on one page.
properties.body:
A multilingual resource keeps several translations together. Its title, summary, and body can have different text for each language while sharing the same resource identity.

Other fields and connections may be shared. This is why translating a page does not usually require making another article and reconnecting the same images.

The site's enabled languages, public language switch, and fallback rules determine which version visitors receive. Empty translated fields may fall back to another language.

Use language tabs to edit content and the public language switch to check it. The language of the admin buttons is a separate interface preference.

See module#mod_translation for the technical reference.

properties.title: Publication and visibility
properties.summary: Understand the separate decisions behind a visible page.
properties.body:
A page can be saved without being public. These controls answer different questions:

  • Saved: are the changes stored?
  • Published: is the page marked for publication?
  • Publication period: is it within its allowed start and end times?
  • Access: may this visitor see it?
  • Menu or collection membership: where is it listed?
  • Search indexing: may a search engine include it in results?

A visitor normally needs publication, timing, and access to agree. Editors may have permission to view content that visitors cannot.

A menu entry does not grant access, and a no-index request does not make a page private. Test the public URL with the intended audience whenever those distinctions matter.

properties.title: Surveys and forms
properties.summary: Build forms, collect responses, and follow up on what people submit.
properties.body:
Use Zotonic's Survey feature for questionnaires, registration forms, simple requests, and quizzes. Start with a short form, test the respondent journey, and decide who will follow up on the answers.

These tasks apply when Surveys is enabled and your account can edit surveys. The collection below takes you from a first form to results and exports. Your site's design and any special handling can change the final appearance and delivery of responses.

properties.title: Surveys and forms: what you can make
properties.summary: Use surveys for feedback, registrations, simple requests, polls, and quizzes.
properties.body:
Zotonic's Survey feature is a form builder. You can collect feedback, take registrations, ask visitors for information, or create a quiz without writing a separate application.

A form can be a single page or a sequence of question pages.

A form is a page with questions, settings, and saved responses. Its editor has four tabs:

  • Description: the title, introduction, and thank-you text.
  • Settings: answering rules, result display, and email handling.
  • Questions: the fields, answer choices, and pages people complete.
  • Results: submitted answers, charts, and downloads.

For a first form, start with a short registration: name, email address, and a yes/no question. Test it before sharing its address.

Your site must have Surveys enabled, and your account must be allowed to create and edit surveys. Ask your website manager if the Survey category is missing. File uploads and connections to another system need additional attention; do not assume every form stores uploaded files or sends data elsewhere.

You are responsible for the questions and what happens to responses. Before building, decide who will read them, what follow-up respondents can expect, and when the form should close.

properties.title: Creating your first form
properties.summary: Create an unpublished survey and give respondents a clear introduction.
properties.body:
You need permission to create a page in the Survey category.

  1. Choose Make a new page or media, enter a title, and choose Survey.
  2. Leave Published unchecked and create the page.
  3. In Description, write a short introduction: what the form is for, who should complete it, and what happens after submission.
  4. Find the Thank you text explanation in the description's Block panel. Write a message such as “Thank you. We will contact you about your visit.”
  5. Open Questions and add the fields you need.
  6. In Settings, choose Thank you text only for the result shown after submission. Leave any special handling choice unchanged unless your website manager has supplied instructions.
  7. Click Save, then View, and complete a test.

For a practice registration, ask for Your name, Your email address, and Would you like a guided visit? Keep questions short and ask only for information you will use.

Saving a form does not publish it. Even an unpublished preview can store a real test response, so use clearly labelled example data. Confirm the response appears under Results before assuming the form is ready.

properties.title: Adding and arranging questions
properties.summary: Choose field types, set required answers, and keep question names stable.
properties.body:
1. Open the form's Questions tab and click Add question. If there is no question page yet, click Add page first.
  2. Choose the question type in Add a question or block.
  3. Give the question a short, unique name, such as visitor_name or email. This identifies the answer; it is not the wording shown to visitors.
  4. Write the question in the prompt field. Add an explanation when people need help answering.
  5. Select Required, this question must be answered only when the form cannot work without that answer.
  6. For a short-answer field, choose Validation when it must contain an email address, number, phone number, or date.
  7. Use the up/down controls or drag handle to arrange questions. Save and check their order with View.
ChooseFor
Short answerA name or a single value; validation checks its format
Long answerA comment or explanation
Yes or noA clear choice between two answers
Multiple choice or quiz questionOne or several choices, with translatable labels
5-point scaleAgreement with a statement
Header or Text, image, videoInstructions between questions

Keep names unique and unchanged once responses exist. Translate prompts and answer labels, not the names used to identify them.

Only editors can answer makes the field read-only for respondents, but they may still see its prompt and saved answer. It is not a private internal note. Hide from results is a display option, not a guarantee that the answer is never stored or accessible.

A file-upload question belongs on the final question page. The standard result email can carry uploads as attachments, but the file is not a normal stored survey answer. Ask your website manager how files will be delivered and retained before using it.

properties.title: Adding answer choices
properties.summary: Offer clear choices while preserving the values used in stored answers.
properties.body:
Use Multiple choice or quiz question (Thurstone) for a question such as “Which session would you like to attend?”

  1. Add the question and enter its name and prompt.
  2. Choose Single answer possible, Drop-down menu, or Multiple answers possible.
  3. Enter an Answer label for the first choice.
  4. Use Add answer for each extra choice.
  5. Give each choice a unique Stored value, such as morning or afternoon. Keep these values stable if you translate or reword the labels.
  6. Choose whether an answer is required. Save and test every choice.

For a registration, offer “Morning visit” and “Afternoon visit”. Do not enable Quiz or test question unless there are right and wrong answers.

Use multiple answers only when selecting several options makes sense. Add “Other” or “Not applicable” when a forced choice would produce misleading responses.

Submit on clicking an option advances the form as soon as a choice is made. Use it only when respondents need no other input on that question page, and test the resulting flow. Randomize answers changes the display order; avoid it for ordered scales or choices that depend on their position.

Do not reuse an existing stored value for a different meaning after collecting responses. Create a new version of the form when the meaning of the question changes.

properties.title: Splitting a form into pages
properties.summary: Group questions and show respondents only the sections they need.
properties.body:
Use several question pages when a form has distinct sections. Keep a short form on one page unless a split helps the respondent.

  1. Open Questions and click Add page.
  2. Add the questions for that section, with a heading or explanation where useful.
  3. Save and use View to check the Next, Back, and final Submit steps.
  4. In Settings → Progress, choose progress text or a progress bar if it helps people understand the length.

Skip an irrelevant section

A page jump uses a question's name and its stored answer value. For example, give a single-choice question the name visit_type, with stored values guided and independent. Put guided-visit questions on the next page and a question named contact_email at the beginning of the following page.

At the end of the first page, click Add page jump. Enter visit_type == "independent" under if, and contact_email under go to. This skips the guided-visit page for independent visits. Use Go to question to check the destination, then save and test both choices.

Avoid jumps that send people around a loop or past questions everyone must answer. Removing a page also removes its questions. Do not select Remove "Next" button unless you have provided and tested another button that continues the form.

For complex conditions, ask your website manager to review the flow. Test every route, including going back and changing an earlier answer.

properties.title: Choosing how people can respond
properties.summary: Set repeat submissions, saved progress, limits, and the final screen.
properties.body:
Open the form's Settings tab before inviting people to respond.

Under Filling in, choose one mode:

  • Once — submit is final: respondents cannot edit their submitted answer.
  • Once — edit after submit: logged-in respondents can return to edit their own answer. Anonymous respondents cannot use this editing mode after submission.
  • Multiple times: each submission creates another response.

For anonymous respondents, “once” is based on a browser cookie, not verified identity. Another browser or a cleared cookie can appear to be another respondent.

Continue later saves progress before final submission; it is separate from editing a submitted answer. Test returning in the same browser and with the intended login arrangement before promising that progress can be resumed.

Set Maximum number of submissions when the form has a limit, or leave it empty for no limit. Test responses count too. Custom handlers may not store results, which can make limits and repeat-submission checks unavailable; ask your website manager if a special handler is selected.

Under Show after the final submit, choose the thank-you text, the respondent's results, or aggregated results. Use thank-you text for registrations unless respondents have a reason to see results. Review what aggregate output reveals before offering it.

Save the settings and test them as the intended respondent. An administrator may see controls and data that an ordinary respondent cannot.

properties.title: Sending form notifications and confirmations
properties.summary: Notify the responsible team and tell respondents their form was received.
properties.body:
Open Settings → Handling on the survey.

  1. In Mail results to, enter the addresses of the people responsible for following up. Separate addresses with commas.
  2. Enable Send a confirmation email to the respondent if a receipt is useful.
  3. For anonymous visitors, add a short-answer question with the exact name email and validation must be an email address. The visible prompt can be “Your email address”. For logged-in respondents, the system can use their known account email address.
  4. Choose which answers the confirmation includes: all, closed questions only, or no answers. There are separate choices for anonymous and logged-in respondents.
  5. Write the Introduction for confirmation email and save.
  6. Submit a clearly labelled test using an address you control. Check the staff notification and respondent receipt, including their language and answer content.

A thank-you screen confirms the form flow, not delivery to an inbox. If an email is missing, check spam and ask your website manager to inspect delivery. The site must have working outbound email.

A confirmation is not a newsletter subscription. Collect and use addresses for the purpose explained on the form. Avoid including unnecessary personal details in emails, and translate the confirmation text when the form has several languages.

A special form handler may change the normal storage or email behaviour. Confirm that arrangement before relying on either notifications or the Results tab.

properties.title: Testing and publishing a form
properties.summary: Check the entire respondent journey before sharing the form.
properties.body:
Test while the survey is unpublished, using your editor preview. Submitting that preview creates a response when the standard storage handler is used; there is no separate automatic test-results area.

  1. Save and click View. Start the form and read the introduction.
  2. Leave required fields empty and try an invalid email or number. Check that the form explains what to correct.
  3. Complete a valid response using clearly labelled test details. Test each choice, page jump, and language the form supports.
  4. Check the thank-you page and any confirmation emails.
  5. Open Results → Results editor and confirm that the answers were stored as expected.
  6. Check keyboard navigation and a narrow screen. Test saved progress or repeat submissions if enabled.
  7. Remove clearly identified practice responses using the results controls only when you no longer need them. Read the deletion confirmation; do not assume responses have a trash or undo function.
  8. Check the form's publication period and access settings, publish it, then test its address as the intended audience. Use a private window for public forms or a suitable test account for restricted forms.

Check that Deactivated is off and a submission limit has not already been reached. An editor's successful preview does not prove anonymous visitors can respond.

Finally, add a link or menu entry wherever people should find the form. Publishing alone does not put it in navigation. Agree who will check new responses and when they will follow up.

properties.title: Reviewing and following up on responses
properties.summary: Read submitted answers, add internal status notes, and make deliberate corrections.
properties.body:
1. Open the survey's Results tab and choose Results editor.
  2. Find a response by its date and identifying details. Choose View answers to read it.
  3. Set a Status and internal Note if your team uses them. Agree what the colours mean; the default statuses do not define a workflow for you.
  4. Click Save to record the changes.

Read the answers below the internal status and note. Save & Email also sends a message; ordinary Save records your changes without that action.

The status and note are visible only to people who can edit the survey. View answers keeps respondent answers read-only but allows editor-only answers to be completed. Those editor-only answers can be visible to the respondent; use the internal note for internal follow-up.

Use Edit all answers only when correcting the response itself is intended. Check the entire response before saving. Save & Email also sends a message to the respondent; use it deliberately and check the destination. Editor-only answers can be included in this message even when ordinary confirmations omit answers.

The results list can link a response to a person. Check the match carefully; this is separate from creating login credentials.

Use Show charts for summaries of closed questions and Printable list for a readable overview. Charts are not a substitute for reading open comments. A configured special handler may send responses elsewhere instead of saving them here.

Delete only the intended response and read the confirmation. Deleting a response does not recall emails or exported copies.

properties.title: Downloading survey results
properties.summary: Export answers and check what information the file contains.
properties.body:
You need permission to download results, and the site's export feature must be enabled.

  1. Open the survey's Results tab and click Download….
  2. Choose Anonymous to remove respondent identity columns from the export, if appropriate.
  3. Select Status only if the recipients need internal status information and notes. This choice is available to survey editors.
  4. Decide whether to include question prompts as the first row.
  5. Choose Excel (XLSX), CSV, or JSON, then Download.
  6. Open the file and check its question columns, response count, and a known test response before sharing it.

An anonymous export is not necessarily anonymous content. A name or email entered as an answer, or identifying details in free text, can still identify someone. Inspect the actual file before sharing it. The form setting that hides user/browser identifiers does not remove information people type into questions.

Keep exported files where only the intended people can access them. They are independent copies: deleting or correcting a response in Zotonic does not update an earlier download.

Show email addresses and Add to mailinglist are separate tools. Do not add respondents to a newsletter simply because they supplied an address for a registration or request.

properties.title: Changing or closing a form
properties.summary: Protect the meaning of existing responses when a form changes.
properties.body:
Fix small wording errors carefully, then save and check the public form. On a published form, changes can affect people immediately.

Once responses exist, keep question names and stored choice values stable. Renaming a question, deleting it, or assigning a new meaning to an old choice can make earlier responses difficult to interpret. Export a copy before a significant revision. For a new round or different questions, make a separate form, review its settings and connections, and check that its Results view has the intended starting state.

Stop accepting responses

  1. Open Settings and select Deactivated.
  2. Save and check the form as an ordinary visitor.
  3. Update the introduction or the page linking to it so people understand that responses are closed.
  4. Keep the survey available to the team that needs its results.

Deactivation stops answering without being the same as unpublishing the page. Unpublish instead when ordinary visitors should no longer see the page itself. A publication end date can also end public access. Test the intended outcome; do not use an event's date range as a form-closing control.

Closing a form does not erase its responses or revoke downloads and emails. Decide separately which records to retain, export, or delete under your team's handling procedures.

properties.title: Creating a quiz
properties.summary: Mark correct answers, set scores, and choose the feedback respondents see.
properties.body:
Start with Multiple choice or quiz question (Thurstone) when you need scored answers.

  1. Add a question, its answer choices, and their unique stored values.
  2. Check Quiz or test question.
  3. Mark the correct choices under Correct and set their Points.
  4. Choose whether only one answer or multiple answers are possible.
  5. Add correct/incorrect feedback where useful. Enable Instant feedback (Learning Mode) only when people should see feedback while answering.
  6. In the survey's Settings, set Test pass percentage and choose the result shown after submission.
  7. Save and test an all-correct response, an incorrect response, and a response near the pass threshold. Check the stored points and the final feedback.

Multiple-answer scoring can award points both for selecting correct choices and for not selecting wrong choices. Subtract points for wrong answers also penalizes omissions of correct choices; an individual question's score does not go below zero. Check the scoring with examples rather than assuming it is one point per question.

Matching questions can provide correctness feedback, but currently do not add points to the stored total. Do not mix them into a scored quiz without accounting for that distinction.

If you show results only after a pass, test both passing and failing outcomes so respondents receive a useful completion message in either case.

properties.title: Getting started
properties.summary: Build a local site and make your first working change.
properties.body:
Start with Set up a local development environment. It gives you a short path through installation, a running blog, and your first visible template change.

Choose one installation route: containers for a first try, native macOS/Linux when you want the tools installed locally, or Nix if you already use it. Each route leads back to the same garden example. The requirements and database pages are supporting instructions; you do not need to read every page before starting.

Once the first edit works, add a dynamic page and explore the development workflow. The collection below also provides the individual setup tasks for later reference.

properties.title: Build and start Zotonic
properties.summary: Compile Zotonic, start it, check the status page, and continue to your first site.
properties.body:
Complete one installation route first. For a native or Nix setup, the tools and database connection should now be ready. Container users whose node is already running can go straight to Create your first site.

1. Build

From the Zotonic repository root, as your normal user:

make

The first build downloads dependencies and compiles Zotonic. Wait for the successful-compilation message. If it fails, resolve the first build error before continuing; a missing compiler or wrong Erlang version is a setup issue.

2. Start

For the first walkthrough, start in the background so the same terminal remains available:

bin/zotonic start
bin/zotonic status

Expect a running node and sites with their states. Open the local status site. This is the installation's management page, not your new website. The initial HTTPS certificate is self-signed; accept it only for this local development address.

If the node is already running, use status rather than starting a second instance. If startup fails, check whether ports 8000/8443 are occupied and read the reported log location.

3. Create a site

Continue with Create your first site. Keep using this repository root for bin/zotonic commands.

Foreground development and stopping

For startup output and an interactive Erlang shell, use bin/zotonic debug instead of start, with Zotonic stopped first. Run further OS commands from a second terminal in the same environment. Do not type shell commands such as bin/zotonic status at the Erlang prompt.

Use bin/zotonic stop to stop this installation. Attach to an existing node with bin/zotonic shell; Ctrl-C twice detaches that remote shell without stopping the node. See startup modes for details.

properties.title: Create your first site
properties.summary: Create the garden blog, open it in your browser, and sign in to its admin.
properties.body:
Start with a running Zotonic node from your installation route. Run the commands below from the repository root, inside the container or Nix shell if you chose one.

1. Create the example site

bin/zotonic addsite -s blog -H garden.test garden
bin/zotonic status

The command creates apps_user/garden, prepares the database schema, compiles the application, and starts it on the running node. Expect garden to reach the running state. Keep the generated admin password shown in the output; you need it for the next step.

2. Give your browser the local hostname

On the computer running your browser, add this line to its hosts file using an administrator-enabled text editor:

127.0.0.1 garden.test

The file is /etc/hosts on macOS/Linux and C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows. For containers, edit the computer's hosts file, not just the container's. Keep any existing entries. You can skip this step if your local DNS already resolves garden.test to this machine.

3. Open the site and admin

Open your garden site in the browser. These examples use the default development HTTPS port 8443; use your configured port if different. Expect the blog home page. The generated development certificate may need a local browser exception.

Open the garden admin and log in as admin, using the password printed by addsite. These are your site's credentials, separate from the status site's wwwadmin account.

4. Make your first change

Open apps_user/garden in your editor, then follow Change a template and see the result. There is no need to create a custom module first.

If the wrong site opens, check the hosts entry and priv/zotonic_site.config hostname. If creation fails, read the error and inspect the partially created directory before retrying. Native database problems can be checked with Prepare local PostgreSQL; containers use database host postgres. See addsite options for a non-default configuration.

properties.title: Change a template and see the result
properties.summary: Make a small visible change before building a larger feature.
properties.body:
With the garden blog running, change its home page. For the blog skeleton used in this walkthrough, the file is apps_user/garden/priv/templates/home.tpl.

  1. Open that file in your editor on your computer.
  2. Find {% block content %} and add this paragraph immediately below it, before the existing content:
<p>{_ Welcome to the community garden. _}</p>
  1. Save the file. In a container setup, the edited checkout is already mounted into the container.
  2. Reload the home page. Expect Welcome to the community garden. above the blog content.

You have now built Zotonic, created a site, and changed a rendered page. Try changing the sentence once more to see the edit–reload cycle.

If the change does not appear, check that you edited apps_user/garden, not _build, and that the browser uses the garden hostname. Check file watching and the development logs for template errors. Sites created with a different skeleton may use another template; use template selection to find it.

Continue with Add your first dynamic page when you want to create a new route.

properties.title: Add your first dynamic page
properties.summary: Use an existing controller and a template for a simple dynamic page.
properties.body:
Use an existing controller and a template for a simple dynamic page.

For a new dispatch file, use the complete list below. In an existing dispatch list, insert the tuple before broader matching rules and separate entries with commas:

[
    {garden_welcome, ["welcome"], controller_template,
        [{template, "garden_welcome.tpl"}]}
].

Create priv/templates/garden_welcome.tpl:

{% extends "base.tpl" %}
{% block content %}
    <h1>{_ Welcome _}</h1>
    <p>{{ m.site.title|escape }}</p>
{% endblock %}

Confirm that your generated base.tpl has a content block; adapt the block name if it differs. Reload /welcome on the site's configured hostname and check that the site title appears.

Use {% url garden_welcome %} to link to this route. For ordinary CMS content, prefer resource page URLs instead of inventing a dispatch rule per page. See Follow a request to its template and Link to resources and dispatch routes.

Save the dispatch list as apps_user/garden/priv/dispatch/garden (create the directory if needed). Save the template under apps_user/garden/priv/templates/. After file handling has refreshed the rules, run bin/zotonic dispatch garden /welcome; expect the garden_welcome rule and controller_template before checking the browser.

properties.title: Understand the development workflow
properties.summary: Work in small, verifiable steps: change source, compile or reload, reproduce the request, and inspect the result.
properties.body:
Work in small, verifiable steps: change source, compile or reload, reproduce the request, and inspect the result.

Templates and dispatch files are indexed per site. Erlang modules are loaded into the shared node. Database changes, module activation, and schema migrations have their own lifecycles; saving a file does not necessarily perform them.

After each change, check the layer involved. A successful Erlang compilation does not prove a URL matches the intended controller. A rendered template does not prove an anonymous visitor has permission to see its data.

Use a named example resource and a repeatable URL while developing. Keep test content separate from imported or production content. Finish with the relevant automated checks and a browser check when behavior is visible.

properties.title: Understanding Zotonic applications
properties.summary: Know where files belong and how sites and modules fit together.
properties.body:
Know where files belong and how sites and modules fit together.

Choose the task that matches what you need to do. The pages explain the relevant workflow and link to related guides and reference material. Examples use the local site garden; use your own site name and check the command’s scope before running it.

properties.title: Erlang applications, Zotonic modules, and sites
properties.summary: These terms describe different parts of the system.
properties.body:
These terms describe different parts of the system.

Putting a package on the code path is different from activating its Zotonic module for a particular site. Use Application startup and per-site module activation to understand this distinction when a compiled feature is missing.

An Erlang application is a package described by a .app file, normally generated from src/<name>.app.src. It can provide modules and an OTP application callback.

A Zotonic module is functionality that can be activated for a site. Its main Erlang module declares attributes such as -mod_title and -mod_depends.

A site is a named website with its own configuration and runtime context. Several sites share the same Erlang VM and loaded code, while module activation and site data are site-specific.

properties.title: Anatomy of a site application
properties.summary: A typical site contains the following directories. Create only the extension directories you actually need.
properties.body:
A typical site contains the following directories. Create only the extension directories you actually need.

garden/
├── rebar.config
├── src/
│   ├── garden.app.src
│   ├── garden.erl
│   ├── controllers/
│   ├── models/
│   ├── filters/
│   ├── scomps/
│   ├── actions/
│   ├── validators/
│   └── support/
└── priv/
    ├── zotonic_site.config
    ├── dispatch/
    ├── templates/
    ├── lib/
    ├── lib-src/
    └── translations/

garden.erl contains the site's Zotonic module declarations and lifecycle hooks. A generated site can also have an OTP application callback and supervisor when created with that option.

Keep template-facing business operations in models and focused implementation helpers in support. Do not turn the main site module into a collection of unrelated functions. See What belongs in src and priv.

properties.title: Anatomy of a reusable module
properties.summary: A reusable module normally lives in apps_user/zotonic_mod_garden and contains:
properties.body:
A reusable module normally lives in apps_user/zotonic_mod_garden and contains:

zotonic_mod_garden/
├── rebar.config
├── src/
│   ├── zotonic_mod_garden.app.src
│   ├── mod_garden.erl
│   └── models/m_garden.erl
└── priv/
    └── templates/

The package name is zotonic_mod_garden; the module activated on a site is mod_garden. Use a .app.src whose application name matches the package.

Add controllers, dispatch rules, translations, and assets only when the feature requires them. A template-only feature does not need a custom process. A background service needs an explicit lifecycle and supervision design.

Build the package, make it discoverable, then activate it for the intended site. See Create a reusable module and Application startup and per-site module activation.

properties.title: Application and module names
properties.summary: Use distinct, consistent names so code and assets can be found without ambiguity.
properties.body:
Use distinct, consistent names so code and assets can be found without ambiguity.

For a reusable feature:

  • Directory/application: zotonic_mod_garden
  • Main Zotonic module: mod_garden
  • Model: m_garden
  • Controller: controller_garden_export
  • Filter: filter_garden_label
  • Site-specific template: garden_overview.tpl

Erlang module names are global within a VM. Two sites cannot load different implementations under the same Erlang module name and expect isolation.

Actions, validators, and scomps use Zotonic's naming conventions, including the owning site/module component. Inspect an existing implementation before naming a new one. Templates can intentionally share names to participate in module-priority overrides; ordinary helper Erlang modules should not.

properties.title: Site configuration and enabled modules
properties.summary: A site is identified by its application and priv/zotonic_site configuration. Supported formats include Erlang .config, JSON, and YAML; follow the format already used by the project.
properties.body:
A site is identified by its application and priv/zotonic_site configuration. Supported formats include Erlang .config, JSON, and YAML; follow the format already used by the project.

For Erlang configuration, the file is a list of terms ending with a period:

[
    {enabled, true},
    {environment, development},
    {hostname, "garden.test"}
].

This is a small fragment illustrating syntax, not a replacement for the generated database and module settings.

Inspect the actual configuration sources with siteconfigfiles garden and siteconfig garden. A site's installation module list and its current activation state are different concerns, especially on database-backed sites. Verify enabled modules in the admin or module manager.

properties.title: Dependencies, capabilities, and module priority
properties.summary: The main site or module can declare:
properties.body:
The main site or module can declare:

-mod_depends([mod_base]).
-mod_prio(500).

Dependencies express requirements for activation. Modules can also declare provided capabilities with -mod_provides; depend on an established capability when your feature requires that service rather than one particular implementation.

Priority determines ordering when modules supply competing resources such as templates. Lower numerical priorities take precedence. Sites commonly use a low priority so their templates override generic module templates.

Do not use priority to hide a missing dependency or duplicate Erlang module name. Check which modules are active, inspect the selected template, and make one intentional override at a time.

properties.title: How Zotonic finds templates, dispatch rules, and assets
properties.summary: Zotonic indexes resources from the site's active modules. A file existing on disk is not enough: its application must be discoverable, and its module must participate in that site.
properties.body:
Zotonic indexes resources from the site's active modules. A file existing on disk is not enough: its application must be discoverable, and its module must participate in that site.

  1. Confirm that the application is included by the umbrella build.
  2. Compile it and inspect any .app.src errors.
  3. Rescan modules when adding a package.
  4. Activate its Zotonic module for the site.
  5. Check template selection or dispatch inspection for the specific resource.

File watching normally picks up edits and additions in known applications. Adding a whole application can need a rescan or broader update. Do not assume the browser cache is responsible until the server selects the correct source file.

properties.title: Application startup and per-site module activation
properties.summary: OTP application startup concerns the application and its processes. Zotonic module activation concerns the feature within an individual site.
properties.body:
OTP application startup concerns the application and its processes. Zotonic module activation concerns the feature within an individual site.

A module can be compiled and available to the VM but inactive on garden. Conversely, activating a module can start per-site behavior, attach observers, and trigger installation or schema work. Treat activation as a state-changing operation.

Use an OTP supervisor for application-level services when appropriate. Use the site's/module's supported lifecycle for state that belongs to one site. Pass the correct site context rather than storing a single global site value in a shared process.

When debugging startup, distinguish a missing application, a failed site, an inactive module, and a crashing worker. Each has a different fix. See Run work outside a request.

properties.title: Runtime data and uploaded files
properties.summary: Keep runtime data separate from the application's source and static assets.
properties.body:
Keep runtime data separate from the application's source and static assets.

Site media, generated previews, backups, logs, and caches can live outside the checkout. Their locations depend on the running installation's configuration. Use Zotonic's storage and path APIs rather than assuming a relative directory beside a template.

For media, work through model#media and related storage facilities so metadata, preview generation, access checks, and storage backends remain coordinated. Never replace a file behind the model's back as a normal upload workflow.

When deploying, preserve the site's durable files as well as its database. Rebuilding _build is not a backup or migration strategy for uploaded content.

properties.title: Working from the command line
properties.summary: Use the shell and CLI to inspect and manage a development installation.
properties.body:
Use the shell and CLI to inspect and manage a development installation.

Choose the task that matches what you need to do. The pages explain the relevant workflow and link to related guides and reference material. Examples use the local site garden; use your own site name and check the command’s scope before running it.

properties.title: Start in the foreground or background
properties.summary: Choose a startup mode for the environment:
properties.body:
Choose a startup mode for the environment:

bin/zotonic debug
bin/zotonic start_nodaemon
bin/zotonic start

Run one of these, not all three. debug keeps an interactive Erlang shell in the foreground. start_nodaemon runs in the foreground without that shell, which suits a process supervisor. start runs in the background.

Use bin/zotonic status afterwards to inspect the node and sites. To attach to an existing instance, use shell.

stop stops the Erlang VM and every site on it. restart restarts Zotonic and its sites within the VM. Use site-specific commands for a change that should affect only one site. See Start, stop, and restart a site.

properties.title: Start, stop, and restart a site
properties.summary: Use these commands for one named site:
properties.body:
Use these commands for one named site:

bin/zotonic startsite garden
bin/zotonic restartsite garden
bin/zotonic stopsite garden

They are alternatives for different tasks; do not run the whole block as a setup recipe. The node must be running. A restart can interrupt requests and site-specific workers, so use it deliberately.

After starting or restarting, inspect status, the logs, and a page on the site's configured hostname. Starting a site does not replace missing dependencies or fix invalid configuration.

Use a normal code reload for a small Erlang edit when appropriate. Reserve whole-node stop and restart for changes that need that broader scope. See Compile changed code and load modules.

properties.title: Compile changed code and load modules
properties.summary: Use make for the normal project build. On a running development node, the CLI also provides focused operations:
properties.body:
Use make for the normal project build. On a running development node, the CLI also provides focused operations:

bin/zotonic compile
bin/zotonic compilefile apps_user/garden/src/garden.erl
bin/zotonic load

compile asks the running file handler to compile modified Erlang sources. compilefile targets a file. load invokes the changed-BEAM loading pass; it does not take an individual module selector in the current implementation.

Read compiler output and logs before retesting. A command returning from an asynchronous request does not prove the entire rebuild has finished.

Use update when you need the broader compile/load/cache/index refresh workflow. Do not rebuild or flush everything repeatedly when a source error explains the failure. See Automatic recompilation and file watching.

properties.title: Automatic recompilation and file watching
properties.summary: Zotonic's file handler watches source changes when a supported watcher is available. Erlang, templates, dispatch files, and assets have different handlers.
properties.body:
Zotonic's file handler watches source changes when a supported watcher is available. Erlang, templates, dispatch files, and assets have different handlers.

  1. Start a local development node and inspect watcher startup messages.
  2. Change one known template and save it.
  3. Check the terminal for the expected compile or index activity.
  4. Reload the matching page.
  5. Repeat with one Erlang change if you need to verify compilation and loading.

If nothing happens, check the watcher installation, watched path, and whether the application is known to Zotonic. An SCSS source can also depend on a project's Makefile rather than a generic file-extension handler.

Browser live reload is separate from server recompilation. See Reload the browser after source changes and A saved change does not appear.

properties.title: Inspect global and site configuration
properties.summary: Use the command suited to the question:
properties.body:
Use the command suited to the question:

bin/zotonic configfiles
bin/zotonic configtest
bin/zotonic siteconfigfiles garden
bin/zotonic siteconfig garden

configfiles and siteconfigfiles locate configuration sources. configtest checks global configuration loading. siteconfig prints the site's file-based configuration; it is not a complete dump of every database-backed module setting.

For runtime values, use the relevant model or configuration API in the running context. setconfig changes global runtime Zotonic settings without writing configuration files.

Do not share unredacted configuration output: database passwords and other secrets may be present. See Find the configuration layer to change and Change a runtime setting deliberately.

properties.title: Trace URL dispatch from the command line
properties.summary: Use dispatch inspection to discover why a path selects a particular controller:
properties.body:
Use dispatch inspection to discover why a path selects a particular controller:

bin/zotonic dispatch garden
bin/zotonic dispatch garden detail
bin/zotonic dispatch garden /welcome

The first form lists site rules, the second includes detail, and the third traces a path. You can also pass a full URL to include hostname-based site selection.

Compare the selected rule, controller, options, and any path rewriting with your expectation. Earlier applicable rules can win over a broad catch-all later in the list.

This is a dispatch diagnosis, not a substitute for making the HTTP request and checking authorization and rendering. See Trace a URL through dispatch and A URL reaches the wrong page.

properties.title: Inspect logs and running processes
properties.summary: Use bin/zotonic logtail for the configured console log, or select error or crash when those files are available. The command prints the last 500 lines and exits; it does not follow the log continuously.
properties.body:
Use bin/zotonic logtail for the configured console log, or select error or crash when those files are available. The command prints the last 500 lines and exits; it does not follow the log continuously.

For live process activity, use bin/zotonic etop if the Erlang installation includes the required tool. Identify the process and time period responsible for repeated activity before changing configuration.

Prefer structured logs containing the operation, result, reason on failure, and a useful resource or site identifier. Avoid logging request bodies or tokens as a shortcut to understanding a problem.

A busy process alone does not identify the slow request. Correlate request timing with template, function, and database traces. See Write logs that explain an operation and A page is slow.

properties.title: Test the database connection
properties.summary: Run bin/zotonic connectdb to test a connection using the global Zotonic database configuration. It does not open PostgreSQL’s interactive client and has no site selector in this checkout.
properties.body:
Run bin/zotonic connectdb to test a connection using the global Zotonic database configuration. It does not open PostgreSQL’s interactive client and has no site selector in this checkout.

The command prints connection options, including the password, before testing. Keep that output private. A site can override global database settings, so success does not prove that its own database and schema are available.

For a site-specific investigation, inspect its configuration and use a database client deliberately, or query application data through Zotonic models with the correct context. Prefer models for normal mutations so notifications and cache invalidation remain coordinated.

properties.title: Run tests and site checks
properties.summary: Use the project's test workflow in a dedicated development or test environment. Two CLI entry points have different scopes:
properties.body:
Use the project's test workflow in a dedicated development or test environment. Two CLI entry points have different scopes:

  • runtests starts the configured test runner and accepts test selections.
  • sitetest garden stops the site, drops and uses the z_sitetest database schema, runs site tests, then restarts with normal configuration. Use a disposable test environment and avoid concurrent runs sharing the database.

Read the relevant reference page before choosing arguments. Tests may create or change data; a passing startup check is not a complete test of models, permissions, and browser behavior.

Run a focused test for the change, then the repository's required broader checks. Preserve the first meaningful error and reproduce it with a minimal case rather than repeatedly restarting the whole node.

properties.title: Back up and restore site data
properties.summary: For a site with backup support enabled:
properties.body:
For a site with backup support enabled:

bin/zotonic backup garden list
bin/zotonic backup garden start
